budget-accounting-and-public-saving.title: Budget Accounting and Public Saving
budget-accounting-and-public-saving.description: Analyze budget balances, revenues, outlays, public saving, and fiscal accounting identities.

easy.q: When federal outlays exceed federal revenues during a fiscal year, what is the result?
options: A budget deficit
A budget surplus
A balanced budget
A reduction in gross debt
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
easy.feedback: A deficit occurs because annual outlays are greater than annual revenues.

easy.q: Which fiscal position exists when annual federal revenues exceed annual outlays?
options: A budget deficit
A budget surplus
A balanced budget
A debt rollover
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
easy.feedback: Revenues greater than outlays produce a positive budget balance, called a surplus.

easy.q: Why is federal borrowing not classified as federal revenue in budget accounting?
options: It counts as revenue when interest rates fall
It becomes a transfer payment received by households
It finances a shortfall rather than counting as revenue
It is included in government purchases when debt is issued
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
easy.feedback: Debt issuance supplies financing, but it does not turn the borrowed funds into budget revenue.

easy.q: In the identity public saving = T − G, what must T represent in this accounting framework?
options: Net tax revenue after relevant transfers
Total federal outlays including transfers and net interest
Gross tax collections before subtracting any transfer payments
The accumulated federal debt stock at a specific date
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
easy.feedback: The shorthand is valid here only when T is defined net of transfers and G is government purchases.

easy.q: Under public saving = T − G, with T defined as net tax revenue and G as government purchases, what does negative public saving mean?
options: Private saving must also be below zero
T is less than G
Nominal GDP must be declining during the year
The government can have no outstanding federal debt
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
easy.feedback: Public saving is negative when net tax revenue T is below government purchases G.

easy.q: A Social Security benefit payment is best classified as what from the federal budget perspective?
options: Federal revenue from payroll taxes
Government purchases included in GDP when paid
Intragovernmental holdings of federal debt
A transfer payment within federal outlays
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
easy.feedback: The payment is an outlay that transfers income; it is not a purchase of current output when issued.

easy.q: The federal government buys newly produced rescue equipment. How is the transaction classified?
options: An outlay and a government purchase
A transfer payment without a current purchase
Federal revenue
Debt held by the public
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
easy.feedback: Paying for newly produced equipment is both an outlay and government purchases in GDP.

medium.q: Federal revenues are $4.8 trillion and outlays are $6.2 trillion. Using revenues minus outlays, what is the budget balance?
options: +$1.4 trillion
−$11.0 trillion
+$11.0 trillion
−$1.4 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
medium.feedback: Revenues minus outlays equals $4.8 trillion minus $6.2 trillion, or −$1.4 trillion, a deficit.

medium.q: A federal budget balance is reported as +$120 billion. What does the positive sign mean?
options: Revenues exceed outlays by $120 billion
Outlays exceed revenues by $120 billion
Federal debt equals $120 billion
Borrowing increased by exactly $120 billion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
medium.feedback: Under the stated revenues-minus-outlays convention, a positive balance is a surplus.

medium.q: Federal revenues total $5.1 trillion and outlays total $5.9 trillion. What is the deficit expressed as a positive magnitude?
options: −$0.8 trillion
$0.8 trillion
$5.1 trillion
$11.0 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
medium.feedback: Outlays exceed revenues by $0.8 trillion, so the deficit magnitude is reported as positive $0.8 trillion.

medium.q: Net tax revenue T is $3.2 trillion and government purchases G are $3.8 trillion. What is public saving?
options: +$0.6 trillion
$3.2 trillion
−$0.6 trillion
$7.0 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
medium.feedback: Using the stated identity, public saving is T minus G, or $3.2 trillion minus $3.8 trillion.

medium.q: Suppose T is explicitly defined as net tax revenue and equals $2.9 trillion, while government purchases G equal $2.5 trillion. What is public saving?
options: −$0.4 trillion
$2.5 trillion
$5.4 trillion
+$0.4 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
medium.feedback: With the variables defined, T − G equals +$0.4 trillion, indicating positive public saving.

medium.q: Which statement accurately distinguishes mandatory and discretionary spending?
options: Mandatory spending cannot change
Mandatory follows standing law; discretionary depends on appropriations
Discretionary spending has no economically important uses
Every federal transfer payment belongs to discretionary spending
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
medium.feedback: The labels describe budget processes, not whether spending matters or can ever be changed by law.

medium.q: Interest paid on outstanding federal debt belongs in which budget category?
options: Federal revenue from outstanding Treasury securities
A transfer payment counted as government purchases in GDP
Net interest outlays, not government purchases
Intragovernmental holdings in federal trust-fund accounts
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
medium.feedback: Interest outlays service prior borrowing; they are not purchases of newly produced goods and services.

hard.q: One table reports a budget balance of −$900 billion; another describes a deficit of $900 billion. Are the reports consistent?
options: No; both reports must show the shortfall with a negative sign
No; balance and deficit figures cannot have the same magnitude
Yes; one is signed and the other gives the deficit magnitude
Yes; both figures describe a $900 billion budget surplus
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
hard.feedback: A negative revenues-minus-outlays balance and a positive deficit magnitude can describe the same shortfall.

hard.q: Revenues rise from $4.9 trillion to $5.2 trillion while outlays rise from $6.0 trillion to $6.1 trillion. How does the budget balance change?
options: It worsens by $0.2 trillion
It improves by $0.3 trillion and becomes a budget surplus
It remains unchanged as both rise
It improves by $0.2 trillion but remains negative
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
hard.feedback: The balance moves from −$1.1 trillion to −$0.9 trillion, an improvement of $0.2 trillion.

hard.q: A table gives total federal revenues of $5 trillion and total outlays, including transfers and interest, of $6 trillion. What should revenues minus outlays be called?
options: A $1 trillion federal budget deficit
Public saving of −$1 trillion under T − G
Private saving of $1 trillion
Government purchases of $6 trillion
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
hard.feedback: Total revenues minus total outlays is the budget balance. In the T − G public-saving shorthand, T must be net tax revenue and G must be government purchases.

hard.q: Holding the relevant definitions and other items fixed, what is the basic public-saving implication of a larger budget deficit?
options: Public saving is necessarily higher
Public saving is lower
Private saving becomes zero by identity
Government purchases are no longer part of GDP
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
hard.feedback: A wider fiscal shortfall reduces the government's contribution to national saving under the introductory accounting link.

hard.q: A benefit payment and a purchase of new federal vehicles are both outlays. What distinguishes their GDP treatment?
options: Both enter G
Neither enters GDP
Only the benefit payment enters G directly when Treasury pays it
Only the vehicle purchase enters G when paid
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
hard.feedback: A transfer redistributes income, whereas the vehicle purchase pays for current production.

hard.q: Taxes raise $4.7 trillion and borrowing supplies $1.1 trillion. Which amount is federal revenue?
options: $4.7 trillion
$1.1 trillion
$5.8 trillion
Neither amount
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
hard.feedback: Taxes are receipts; borrowing finances the gap and is not recorded as revenue.

elite.q: A published table rounds revenues to $5.6 trillion, outlays to $7.4 trillion, and the deficit to $1.9 trillion. Why need the rounded entries not subtract exactly?
options: The displayed figures were rounded independently
The deficit excludes displayed revenues
Borrowing is added to both displayed revenues and displayed outlays
The deficit uses calendar-year data
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
elite.feedback: Independent rounding can make displayed components differ slightly from an identity calculated with unrounded values.

elite.q: A budget worksheet reports $920 billion of cash inflows, including $180 billion from issuing new debt, and $870 billion of total outlays. All remaining inflows are revenues; there are no other financing adjustments. What are the budget balance and the amount of new borrowing left to increase cash balances?
options: A $50 billion surplus and no borrowing needed for the outlays
A $130 billion deficit and a $50 billion cash increase
A $130 billion deficit and a $180 billion cash increase
A $310 billion deficit and a $130 billion cash decrease
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
elite.feedback: Revenues exclude borrowing: 920 − 180 = $740 billion. Revenues minus outlays equal 740 − 870 = −$130 billion. Of the $180 billion borrowed, $130 billion finances the deficit and $50 billion increases cash balances.

elite.q: A simplified fiscal account reports gross tax receipts of $900 billion, transfers of $180 billion, government purchases of $660 billion and interest payments of $70 billion. These are all revenues and outlays. For this exercise define T as gross taxes minus transfers, excluding interest. Which pair gives textbook public saving T − G and the full budget balance?
options: Public saving is $240 billion; the full budget has a $60 billion surplus
Public saving is −$10 billion; the full budget also has a $10 billion deficit
Public saving is $60 billion; the full budget has a $10 billion deficit
Public saving is $60 billion; the full budget has a $60 billion surplus
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
elite.feedback: Under the stated convention, T = 900 − 180 = $720 billion and T − G = $60 billion. Total outlays are 180 + 660 + 70 = $910 billion, giving a $10 billion deficit. The $70 billion difference is interest, which this exercise excludes from net taxes. Transfers are already deducted in T and must not be deducted a second time.

elite.q: A speaker calls all discretionary outlays “optional” and all mandatory outlays “uncontrollable.” What is wrong with the claim?
options: Discretionary outlays are made without any congressional appropriations
The labels describe funding rules, not permanence or importance
Mandatory programs never transfer
Net interest outlays are classified as federal budget revenues
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
elite.feedback: Process labels do not settle importance, desirability, or whether future law can alter spending.

legendary.q: A government starts the year with $3,600 billion of debt. Revenues are $760 billion and outlays are $940 billion. It issues $500 billion of debt, including debt used to repay $270 billion of maturing principal; remaining financing may change cash balances. With no other debt or financing adjustments, which reconciliation is correct?
options: A $180 billion deficit, ending debt of $4,100 billion, and a $320 billion increase in cash
A $320 billion surplus, ending debt of $3,830 billion, and a $50 billion increase in cash
A $180 billion deficit, ending debt of $3,830 billion, and a $50 billion increase in cash
A $450 billion deficit, ending debt of $3,780 billion, and unchanged cash
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
legendary.feedback: The deficit is 940 − 760 = $180 billion; debt issuance is financing, not revenue. Net issuance is 500 − 270 = $230 billion, so ending debt is $3,830 billion. Net financing exceeds the deficit by $50 billion, increasing cash. Principal repayment is not counted again as a budget outlay.

boss.q: Annual federal revenues equal $5.0 trillion and outlays equal $5.3 trillion. Which fiscal position is shown?
options: A $0.3 trillion surplus
A balanced budget
A $5.3 trillion debt stock
A $0.3 trillion deficit
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
boss.feedback: Outlays exceed revenues by $0.3 trillion, so the annual budget is in deficit.

boss.q: According to CBO's February 2026 baseline, FY2026 revenues are projected at about $5.6 trillion and outlays at about $7.4 trillion. What fiscal position is projected?
options: A deficit because projected outlays exceed projected revenues
A surplus because projected revenues are positive
A balanced budget because both values are projections
A debt stock of $1.8 trillion
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
boss.feedback: CBO projects outlays above revenues, which is a deficit; the published rounded deficit is about $1.9 trillion.

boss.q: With T defined as net tax revenue and G as government purchases, T equals $800 billion and G equals $900 billion. What is public saving?
options: +$100 billion
$800 billion
$1.7 trillion
−$100 billion
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
boss.feedback: T − G equals −$100 billion, so public saving is negative.

boss.q: Which statement uses the public-saving convention correctly?
options: T − G, with T net of transfers and G purchases
Total revenues minus all federal outlays is always T − G public saving
T means gross collections and G includes transfers
Public saving is the federal debt stock
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
boss.feedback: The notation is valid only when T is net tax revenue, net of transfers, and G is government purchases.

boss.q: The government collects payroll taxes, sends pension benefits, and buys medical equipment. Which classification is correct?
options: Taxes, benefits, and equipment purchases are all federal revenue
Benefits and equipment both enter government purchases in GDP when paid
Taxes are revenue; both payments are outlays; only equipment is G
Payroll taxes are borrowing
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
boss.feedback: Budget and GDP classifications overlap but are not identical: transfers are outlays without entering G when paid.

legendaryBoss.q: A simplified government has only three outlay categories: purchases of current domestic goods and services, transfers, and interest. Purchases rise from $400 billion to $430 billion, transfers from $300 billion to $350 billion, and interest from $50 billion to $70 billion. Revenues rise by $60 billion. Which comparison is correct?
options: The deficit widens by $40 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $100 billion
The deficit narrows by $30 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $40 billion
The deficit widens by $100 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $30 billion
The deficit widens by $40 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $30 billion
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Outlays rise by 30 + 50 + 20 = $100 billion. With revenues up $60 billion, the deficit widens $40 billion. Only the $30 billion increase in current purchases directly increases G; transfers and interest are budget outlays without being current government purchases. No induced output response is being calculated.

repairQuestions.q: Federal revenues are $5 trillion and outlays are $6 trillion. Is the budget in surplus or deficit?
options: Surplus
Deficit
Balanced
Debt-free
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
repairQuestions.feedback: Outlays exceed revenues by $1 trillion, so the federal budget is in deficit.

repairQuestions.q: T is net tax revenue of $700 billion and G is purchases of $600 billion. What is public saving?
options: −$100 billion
+$100 billion
$600 billion
$1.3 trillion
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
repairQuestions.feedback: Subtract government purchases from net tax revenue: $700 billion minus $600 billion equals +$100 billion.

repairQuestions.q: Which transaction is a government purchase rather than a transfer?
options: The federal purchase of new computers
A pension benefit payment
An unemployment benefit payment
An interest payment on debt
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
repairQuestions.feedback: Buying current goods is a government purchase; benefits and interest are outlays but not G purchases.

bridgeQuestions.q: A federal budget records revenues below outlays. What financing issue follows from that accounting result?
options: The shortfall becomes additional tax revenue in the same year
Government purchases become zero
The shortfall must be financed, commonly through borrowing
Existing federal debt disappears
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A deficit is an annual financing gap; borrowing is a common way to cover it.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does negative public saving matter beyond the federal budget?
options: It directly fixes the economy's nominal exchange rate
It makes positive private saving impossible by definition
It reduces one component of national saving
It determines the national money supply without monetary policy
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Negative public saving lowers national saving, all else equal, and therefore reduces the funds available to finance investment in the loanable-funds model.

bridgeQuestions.q: A federal benefit payment is an outlay but not government purchases in GDP when paid. When can it affect measured GDP?
options: When Treasury classifies the benefit as mandatory spending
When recipients buy newly produced goods or services
Immediately, because every federal outlay enters G in GDP
Only after the outstanding federal debt stock begins to fall
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The transfer itself is not production; later consumption of current final output can enter GDP.

deficits-debt-and-government-borrowing.title: Deficits, Debt, and Government Borrowing
deficits-debt-and-government-borrowing.description: Distinguish deficits from debt and analyze persistent deficits and government borrowing.

easy.q: Which statement correctly classifies the federal deficit and federal debt?
options: Deficit and debt: both annual fiscal flows
Deficit and debt: both accumulated fiscal stocks
Deficit: accumulated stock; debt: annual flow
Deficit: annual flow; debt: accumulated stock
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
easy.feedback: A deficit is measured over a period, while debt is measured at a point in time.

easy.q: The federal deficit falls from $1.8 trillion to $1.2 trillion. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Borrowing needs are smaller, but debt can still rise
Federal debt falls by the $0.6 trillion reduction in the deficit
The budget moves into surplus
Existing federal debt is eliminated
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
easy.feedback: A smaller positive deficit adds less to debt than before, but it still represents a shortfall.

easy.q: What does a balanced annual federal budget imply about existing federal debt?
options: It immediately reduces the accumulated debt stock to zero
It prevents a new deficit but does not erase existing debt
It proves the preceding fiscal year ended with a surplus
It reclassifies all existing federal debt as current revenue
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
easy.feedback: Balancing annual revenues and outlays addresses the current flow, not the accumulated stock.

easy.q: What generally happens when the federal government runs persistent deficits?
options: They automatically erase existing debt
Every annual deficit becomes an equal surplus in a later year
They generally add to accumulated debt
Government purchases are removed from measured GDP during deficit years
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
easy.feedback: Deficits are recurring gaps that generally require financing and add to the debt stock.

easy.q: Which sequence is correct at an introductory level?
options: Surplus, lower revenue, larger deficit by definition
Debt, automatic revenue, no outlays
Borrowing, smaller debt, larger surplus by identity
Deficit, financing through borrowing, larger accumulated debt
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
easy.feedback: Borrowing commonly finances a deficit, and repeated borrowing adds to outstanding debt.

medium.q: Assume a $400 billion deficit is entirely financed by borrowing and there are no other financing adjustments. What happens to federal debt?
options: It falls by $400 billion
It is unchanged
It rises by $400 billion
It becomes exactly $400 billion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
medium.feedback: Under the stated simplifying assumption, borrowing to finance the deficit adds $400 billion to the debt stock.

medium.q: A deficit declines from $900 billion to $500 billion. Has the budget moved into surplus?
options: Yes; the deficit fell by $400 billion
Yes; any deficit reduction is a surplus
No; a surplus is impossible when revenues rise
No; outlays still exceed revenues by $500 billion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
medium.feedback: Reducing a deficit changes its size, but a surplus requires revenues to exceed outlays.

medium.q: Assume there are no other financing adjustments. How can an annual surplus affect federal debt?
options: The surplus can be used to reduce the debt stock
It must increase debt by the surplus amount
It converts debt from a stock into a flow
It leaves debt unchanged by definition
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
medium.feedback: With revenues above outlays, the excess can reduce outstanding borrowing under the stated assumption.

medium.q: Debt is initially $12 trillion. Three annual deficits of $0.4 trillion are fully financed by borrowing, with no other adjustments. What is debt afterward?
options: $13.2 trillion
$10.8 trillion
$12.4 trillion
$14.4 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
medium.feedback: Three deficits add $1.2 trillion to the starting stock under the simplifying assumptions.

medium.q: Why does issuing debt not close a deficit by increasing measured revenue?
options: It counts as mandatory spending in the federal budget
It finances the deficit but is not revenue
It reduces current federal outlays to zero when issued
It represents only borrowing from intragovernmental accounts
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
medium.feedback: Financing explains how the shortfall is covered, not how revenues and outlays are classified.

hard.q: Debt begins at $18.0 trillion. Deficits of $0.8 trillion and $0.5 trillion follow in two years. Assuming borrowing finances each deficit and no other adjustments occur, what is debt after year two?
options: $17.7 trillion
$19.3 trillion
$18.5 trillion
$20.6 trillion
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
hard.feedback: The two deficits add $1.3 trillion to the initial $18.0 trillion debt stock.

hard.q: A report says debt reached $25 trillion while the year's deficit was $1 trillion. Why are the figures not contradictory?
options: The annual deficit excludes most categories of federal outlays
Debt measures only interest payments
Debt is a stock; the deficit is an annual flow
Debt and deficit figures must become equal after each fiscal year
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
hard.feedback: The annual deficit is one contributor to the much larger accumulated debt stock.

hard.q: Why is the reported annual deficit not always identical to the measured change in federal debt?
options: Reported deficits do not require financing through any source
Federal debt is measured only at ten-year intervals
Annual deficit calculations exclude all categories of federal revenue
Financing adjustments can separate the debt change from the deficit
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
hard.feedback: Real Treasury financing includes adjustments beyond the simplified classroom assumption that all deficit financing maps one-for-one into debt.

hard.q: A government raises purchases with net taxes unchanged. Private-saving behavior is unchanged. Which sequence describes the fiscal consequence?
options: Private saving falls but public saving is unchanged, because government purchases are household consumption
Public saving rises and the budget moves toward surplus, reducing the need to issue government debt
Public saving falls and the budget moves toward deficit, increasing borrowing needs if the shortfall is debt-financed
Public saving falls but issuing debt counts as revenue, so borrowing restores the budget balance
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
hard.feedback: With net taxes unchanged, higher government purchases reduce public saving T − G and move the budget toward deficit. Borrowing can finance the shortfall, but debt issuance does not count as revenue or reverse the decline in public saving.

hard.q: Which statement about sustained government borrowing is appropriately conditional?
options: It always eliminates all private investment
It can leave broader financial conditions permanently unaffected in every case
It can guarantee faster economic growth whenever the government borrows
It can raise rates and reduce some private investment
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
hard.feedback: The possible effect depends on economic conditions; it is not an unconditional outcome.

elite.q: A deficit falls from $1.4 trillion to $0.9 trillion while debt rises. Which explanation is coherent?
options: Debt can still rise because the budget remains in deficit
A smaller deficit is a surplus
Debt can rise only when the annual deficit also becomes larger
Debt rose because revenues exceeded outlays
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
elite.feedback: A reduced deficit remains positive borrowing need; it need not reverse the direction of the debt stock.

elite.q: A proposal balances the budget beginning next year. Which claim goes beyond what that fact establishes?
options: No new deficit is planned next year
The existing federal debt will disappear next year
Projected revenues equal projected outlays next year
The annual budget position would improve if it was previously in deficit
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
elite.feedback: A balanced flow prevents new deficit accumulation but does not repay the accumulated stock immediately.

legendary.q: The deficit becomes smaller, nominal debt rises, and debt-to-GDP falls. Which combination can explain all three facts?
options: A surplus raises debt
Debt falls faster than GDP while the annual deficit becomes larger
Debt rises, but nominal GDP grows faster
A balanced budget erases existing debt while nominal GDP remains unchanged
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
legendary.feedback: The deficit can still add to nominal debt, while faster GDP growth lowers the debt ratio.

legendary.q: At year-end a government owes $2,400 billion. During the final month its deficit was $20 billion. An analyst divides 2,400 by 20 and calls the result a 120 percent annual debt-growth rate. If the monthly deficit instead remained constant for a full future year, all deficits were borrowed, and no other debt adjustments occurred, what would the calculation establish?
options: The original quotient is a 120 percent growth rate; annualizing the deficit leaves that rate unchanged
The original quotient is 120 years of deficits; the stated future scenario implies 1 percent annual debt growth
The original quotient is a 10 percent growth rate; dividing it by 12 gives annual debt growth
The original quotient is 120 months of deficits; the stated future scenario implies 10 percent annual debt growth
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
legendary.feedback: A stock of $2,400 billion divided by a flow of $20 billion per month gives 120 months, not a percent growth rate. Under the explicit future assumption, twelve monthly deficits add $240 billion to debt; 240 / 2,400 = 10 percent. One observed month alone does not establish that future path.

legendary.q: Two packages require the same additional borrowing, leave public saving equally lower, and face the same unchanged private-saving and investment-demand schedules. Package A finances productive public infrastructure; Package B finances transfers. What evidence is needed to decide whether A leaves more total productive capital than before the policy?
options: Whether the public-capital addition exceeds the private-capital formation displaced by the higher real rate
Whether A issues less debt than B, even though their additional borrowing is stated to be equal
Whether transfers count as current public-capital formation at the moment they are paid
Whether a decline in public saving is itself a one-for-one measure of lost private capital
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
legendary.feedback: Both packages create the same initial loanable-funds pressure under the stated schedules. A also adds public productive capital. Its net capital effect depends on that addition relative to displaced private capital formation; borrowing alone does not establish the sign. No project-valuation or AD-AS model is needed for this comparison.

boss.q: The annual deficit narrows from $1.5 trillion to $0.7 trillion. Assuming each deficit is financed by borrowing, which statement is correct?
options: Debt rises by less in the second year
Debt falls by $0.8 trillion during the second fiscal year
The second year has a surplus
Debt remains unchanged
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
boss.feedback: Both years have positive deficits, so debt rises under the assumption; only the size of the addition falls.

boss.q: Over four years, the government runs progressively smaller but still positive deficits. Under simplified borrowing finance, what happens?
options: Debt falls each year because every annual deficit is smaller
Debt rises by smaller amounts each year
Debt becomes zero when the fourth and smallest deficit occurs
Public saving becomes positive
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
boss.feedback: A smaller deficit is still a deficit; it adds less to debt but does not reverse the stock by itself.

legendaryBoss.q: CBO's February 2026 baseline projects a $1.9 trillion FY2026 deficit and debt held by the public equal to 101 percent of GDP at year-end. What distinction is essential?
options: Two realized annual flows
A fiscal-year flow versus a year-end stock ratio
A tax-financed share of outlays versus a projected revenue total
The deficit is accumulated debt
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The CBO figures describe different economic objects and are explicitly projections.

legendaryBoss.q: A deficit reduces public saving at every real rate. A separate household incentive exactly offsets that reduction in planned private saving at every rate, while an investment tax credit also raises desired investment. In the closed-economy loanable-funds model, what can be concluded relative to the initial equilibrium?
options: The saving curve shifts left; the real rate rises and private investment must fall
Both curves are unchanged; exact private-saving offset also cancels the investment tax credit
The saving curve is unchanged; the real rate and equilibrium private investment rise
The saving curve shifts right; private investment rises but the real rate must fall
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The public- and private-saving shifts cancel at every rate, leaving national-saving supply unchanged. The tax credit separately shifts investment demand right. With an upward-sloping saving curve, the new equilibrium has a higher real rate and more private investment. A higher rate alone does not prove crowding out when investment demand also changes.

repairQuestions.q: Which measure describes how much outlays exceed revenues during one year?
options: The debt stock
Debt-to-GDP
The deficit
Intragovernmental holdings
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
repairQuestions.feedback: A deficit is measured over a year; debt is the accumulated amount outstanding at a date.

repairQuestions.q: A government has outlays above revenues. What commonly finances the shortfall?
options: A budget surplus
Lower accumulated debt by definition
Government purchases becoming revenue
Government borrowing
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
repairQuestions.feedback: Borrowing is a common way to finance the annual gap between outlays and revenues.

bridgeQuestions.q: A government runs a deficit and finances it entirely by borrowing. What happens next in the simplified example?
options: The debt stock is erased
The budget becomes balanced automatically
The deficit becomes revenue
The debt stock increases
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Borrowing to cover the annual shortfall adds to accumulated debt under the stated simplification.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which framework traces how lower public saving can affect interest rates and private investment?
options: Saving, investment, and loanable funds
The consumer price index and inflation measurement alone
Monopoly pricing
The production-possibilities frontier without financial markets
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The loanable-funds model traces how lower national saving can raise the real interest rate and reduce private investment.

debt-measures-burden-and-fiscal-data.title: Debt Measures, Debt Burden, and Fiscal Data
debt-measures-burden-and-fiscal-data.description: Interpret debt measures, debt-to-GDP, debt service, interest burdens, and real fiscal data.

objectiveLabels.debt-measures-burden-and-fiscal-data: Debt Measures, Debt Burden, and Fiscal Data

easy.q: Which measure covers federal debt held by entities outside the federal government?
options: The intragovernmental debt component
The annual federal budget deficit
Debt held by the public
Annual net interest outlays
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
easy.feedback: Debt held by the public is the portion held outside the federal government under Treasury's definition.

easy.q: What are intragovernmental holdings?
options: Treasury securities held by foreign governments and private investors
The annual federal deficit
Only Federal Reserve currency
Federal securities held in government accounts
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
easy.feedback: They are claims held within federal government accounts, not debt held by outside investors.

easy.q: Debt held by the public is $24 trillion and nominal GDP is $30 trillion. What is debt-to-GDP?
options: 6 percent
80 percent
24 percent
125 percent
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
easy.feedback: Dividing $24 trillion by $30 trillion and multiplying by 100 gives 80 percent.

easy.q: What does debt held by the public equal to 90 percent of GDP mean?
options: Ninety percent of annual federal outlays consist of net interest
The annual federal deficit equals 90 percent of nominal GDP
The debt stock equals 90 percent of one year's GDP
The federal government owns 90 percent of domestic production
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
easy.feedback: The ratio compares a debt stock at a date with the scale of annual economic output.

easy.q: Which statement distinguishes federal debt from annual net interest outlays?
options: Debt is a stock; net interest is an annual outlay
Debt and net interest are both annual federal revenue flows
Net interest equals the entire outstanding federal debt stock
Federal debt is a transfer payment measured during each month
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
easy.feedback: Outstanding debt is measured at a date, while net interest is paid over a budget period.

easy.q: Holding the debt stock fixed, what can raise annual interest costs in a simplified example?
options: A lower average interest rate
A higher average interest rate
A smaller debt stock
A larger budget surplus with no rate change
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
easy.feedback: With the stock held fixed, a higher effective rate raises the interest paid during the year.

easy.q: CBO's February 2026 baseline says the FY2026 deficit is projected at $1.9 trillion. Which wording is accurate?
options: The government has already realized a $1.9 trillion FY2026 deficit
CBO projects a $1.9 trillion FY2026 deficit
Treasury collected a $1.9 trillion surplus
The current federal debt is $1.9 trillion
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Real-World Fiscal-Data Interpretation.
easy.feedback: A baseline published before the fiscal year is complete reports a projection, not a realized result.

easy.q: Treasury's Debt to the Penny dataset reports daily U.S. dollar debt amounts. What does an observation dated August 25, 2026 represent?
options: A completed fiscal-year deficit
A ten-year CBO projection beginning on August 25
A debt stock on August 25, 2026
Federal revenues collected during the month of August
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Real-World Fiscal-Data Interpretation.
easy.feedback: Debt to the Penny records the outstanding debt stock on a specified date; it does not report an annual deficit.

medium.q: Debt held by the public is $24 trillion and intragovernmental holdings are $6 trillion. What is total public debt outstanding?
options: $30 trillion
$18 trillion
$24 trillion
$144 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
medium.feedback: Treasury defines total public debt outstanding as the sum of the two components.

medium.q: Why is a statement that “federal debt is $X” incomplete?
options: Debt can never be measured in dollars
Different federal debt measures can have different values and meanings
Every debt measure equals the annual deficit
Only GDP can be used to describe debt
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
medium.feedback: The statement should identify whether it means debt held by the public, total public debt, or another specified measure.

medium.q: Two countries each have $2 trillion in public debt. Country A's GDP is $4 trillion; Country B's is $10 trillion. Which has the higher debt-to-GDP ratio?
options: Country B
They have equal ratios
The comparison is impossible even with GDP
Country A
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
medium.feedback: The ratios are 50 percent for A and 20 percent for B, so equal nominal debt implies different relative burdens.

medium.q: Debt grows 5 percent while nominal GDP grows 8 percent. What happens to debt-to-GDP, other things equal?
options: It falls
It rises by 13 percent
It rises because nominal debt rose
It is unchanged
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
medium.feedback: The denominator grows faster than the numerator, so debt becomes a smaller share of GDP.

medium.q: Debt-to-GDP rises from 90 percent to 95 percent. How should the change be stated?
options: An increase of exactly 5 percent
An increase of 5 percentage points
An increase of 95 percentage points
A decrease of 5 percentage points
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
medium.feedback: Subtracting percentage levels gives a five-percentage-point increase; the percent change would be about 5.6 percent.

medium.q: Assume, for illustration, that a $10 trillion debt stock carries a uniform 4 percent annual rate. What is the annual interest cost?
options: $4.0 trillion
$40 trillion
$0.4 trillion
$0.04 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
medium.feedback: Under the explicitly simplified assumption, 4 percent of $10 trillion is $0.4 trillion.

medium.q: Net interest outlays are $0.9 trillion and total outlays are $6.0 trillion. What share of outlays is net interest?
options: 6 percent
9 percent
67 percent
15 percent
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
medium.feedback: Dividing $0.9 trillion by $6.0 trillion gives 0.15, or 15 percent.

medium.q: CBO's February 2026 baseline projects FY2026 revenues of $5.6 trillion and outlays of $7.4 trillion. Using the displayed rounded values, what approximate balance is implied?
options: About a $1.8 trillion surplus
About a $13.0 trillion deficit
A balanced budget
About a $1.8 trillion deficit
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Real-World Fiscal-Data Interpretation.
medium.feedback: The displayed values imply outlays exceed revenues by about $1.8 trillion; CBO separately reports a rounded deficit of $1.9 trillion.

hard.q: A report lists debt held by the public at $25 trillion and total public debt outstanding at $32 trillion. What can be inferred?
options: The $7 trillion difference is the annual deficit
The two figures must refer to different countries
The difference reflects intragovernmental holdings under the stated Treasury definitions
Debt held by the public includes all intragovernmental holdings
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
hard.feedback: Total public debt combines debt held by the public with intragovernmental holdings.

hard.q: Why should debt subject to the statutory limit not automatically be substituted for debt held by the public?
options: The debt limit is an annual flow
Debt held by the public excludes every type of Treasury security
Both measures are identical
The measures cover different sets of federal obligations
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
hard.feedback: Debt measures have distinct legal and analytical boundaries, so the label must match the source.

hard.q: Debt rises from $20 trillion to $21 trillion while nominal GDP rises from $20 trillion to $22 trillion. What happens to debt-to-GDP?
options: It rises from 100 percent to 105 percent because debt increases
It remains at 100 percent
It falls from 100 percent to about 95.5 percent
It falls from 100 percent to approximately 50 percent
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
hard.feedback: Debt grows 5 percent, but GDP grows 10 percent, reducing the ratio to approximately 21/22.

hard.q: Economy A has $9 trillion in debt and $12 trillion in GDP. Economy B has $12 trillion in debt and $24 trillion in GDP. Which has the higher debt-to-GDP ratio?
options: Economy B
They are equal
Nominal debt alone makes comparison impossible after GDP is supplied
Economy A
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
hard.feedback: A's ratio is 75 percent, compared with 50 percent for B.

hard.q: Nominal debt rises, yet debt-to-GDP falls. What must be true under the stated comparison?
options: Nominal GDP grew faster than debt
GDP necessarily fell
The annual federal budget necessarily recorded a surplus
Part of the federal debt was reclassified as current revenue
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
hard.feedback: A falling ratio with a rising numerator requires the denominator to grow at a faster proportional rate.

hard.q: Why can rising interest outlays contribute to future deficits, other things equal?
options: They raise outlays without purchasing current services
They can raise tax revenue by the same amount
They reduce the outstanding debt stock as soon as interest is paid
They are excluded from total outlays in federal budget accounting
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
hard.feedback: Higher interest costs widen the gap between revenues and outlays unless offset elsewhere.

hard.q: CBO's February 2026 baseline projects the deficit at 5.8 percent of GDP in 2026 and 6.7 percent in 2036. What is the change?
options: An increase of 0.9 percentage point
An increase of 0.9 percent
An increase of 12.5 percentage points
A decrease of 0.9 percentage point
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Real-World Fiscal-Data Interpretation.
hard.feedback: Subtracting the two projected shares gives 0.9 percentage point.

elite.q: Two releases report different debt values on the same date, but one labels debt held by the public and the other labels total public debt outstanding. What is the best conclusion?
options: The releases use different debt measures
One release must be false
The numerical difference must equal the deficit recorded on that date
The smaller reported figure must represent intragovernmental holdings alone
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
elite.feedback: Measure definitions must be aligned before interpreting a numerical difference.

elite.q: A commentator says Economy B is in the weaker fiscal position because its nominal debt is larger than Economy A's. What evidence is missing?
options: The unemployment rate alone
Comparable GDP and consistently defined debt
Only the total number of public and private bondholders
A complete list of every government agency in both economies
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
elite.feedback: Relative comparisons require both economic scale and consistently defined debt measures.

elite.q: In a simplified debt portfolio, $600 billion remains at a fixed 2 percent annual rate and $400 billion is refinanced from 2 to 5 percent at the start of the year. Principal stays constant; rates apply for the full year and there are no interest receipts. Revenues and noninterest outlays are unchanged. How do interest outlays and the deficit change?
options: Interest outlays become $50 billion and the deficit widens $30 billion
Interest outlays become $32 billion and the deficit widens $12 billion
Interest outlays become $20 billion and the deficit is unchanged
Interest outlays become $32 billion and the deficit widens $32 billion
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
elite.feedback: Initial interest is (600 + 400)(0.02) = $20 billion. New interest is 600(0.02) + 400(0.05) = 12 + 20 = $32 billion. The $12 billion increase widens the deficit by the same amount. The current refinancing rate applies only to the repriced portion, not the whole portfolio.

elite.q: What does CBO's February 2026 baseline projection establish about the future?
options: Fixed future legislation
A conditional benchmark, not a guaranteed forecast
Realized Treasury budget results for every year in the projection window
A projection that eliminates uncertainty about future interest rates
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Real-World Fiscal-Data Interpretation.
elite.feedback: Baseline projections are conditional benchmarks whose outcomes can change with laws, economic conditions, and other developments.

legendary.q: A government begins with debt equal to 80 percent of nominal GDP. During the year it borrows an amount equal to 4 percent of initial GDP to finance its deficit, with no other debt adjustments. Nominal GDP grows 8 percent. Which result reconciles the deficit, the debt stock and the debt ratio?
options: Debt rises 4 percent, and debt-to-GDP falls to exactly 76 percent
Debt falls 4 percent, so debt-to-GDP falls to about 77.8 percent
Debt rises 5 percent, but debt-to-GDP falls to about 77.8 percent
Debt rises 5 percent, so debt-to-GDP rises to 84 percent
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
legendary.feedback: Normalize initial GDP to 100: debt starts at 80, borrowing adds 4 and GDP rises to 108. Debt growth is 4 / 80 = 5 percent; the new ratio is 84 / 108 ≈ 77.8 percent. Faster denominator growth lowers the ratio despite the borrowing-financed deficit.

legendary.q: Debt-to-GDP rises from 80 percent to 88 percent while nominal GDP rises 5 percent. The debt measure and accounting dates are comparable. Which comparison correctly separates the ratio change from the change in nominal debt?
options: The ratio rises 8 percentage points, or 10 percent; nominal debt rises 10 percent
The ratio rises 8 percent, or 10 percentage points; nominal debt rises 13 percent
The ratio rises 8 percentage points, or 10 percent; nominal debt rises 5 percent
The ratio rises 8 percentage points, or 10 percent; nominal debt rises 15.5 percent
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
legendary.feedback: The ratio increases by 8 points and by 8 / 80 = 10 percent relative to its initial level. Nominal debt changes by the ratio factor times the GDP factor: (88 / 80)(1.05) = 1.155, or 15.5 percent. The ratio growth rate is not the numerator growth rate when GDP also changes.

legendary.q: A Treasury observation reports total public debt outstanding, while a CBO projection reports debt held by the public as a percentage of GDP. What must be aligned before comparing them?
options: Only the agency names
Only whether both reported fiscal values have positive signs
Definition, date, status, and units
Nothing, because all federal debt measures and dates are interchangeable
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Real-World Fiscal-Data Interpretation.
legendary.feedback: A sound comparison requires the same measure, date/status, and units.

legendary.q: CBO’s February 2026 baseline gives projected debt-held-by-the-public ratios of 101 percent of GDP in 2026 and 120 percent in 2036. Using only these displayed ratios, when would nominal debt in 2036 exceed nominal debt in 2026?
options: When nominal GDP in 2036 exceeds 120 percent of its 2026 level; a smaller GDP increase implies falling debt
Only when nominal GDP is unchanged; otherwise the two debt ratios cannot be compared
For every possible positive GDP level in 2036; a higher ratio proves a larger nominal debt stock
When nominal GDP in 2036 exceeds about 84.2 percent of its 2026 level; the ratios alone do not establish GDP’s change
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Real-World Fiscal-Data Interpretation.
legendary.feedback: Debt is its GDP share times nominal GDP. Thus 1.20 × GDP2036 must exceed 1.01 × GDP2026, requiring GDP2036 / GDP2026 > 101 / 120 ≈ 0.8417. A higher ratio alone does not identify nominal-debt growth without denominator evidence. This threshold uses the displayed rounded ratios and is not a forecast of GDP.

boss.q: Which expression gives the broad Treasury relationship for total public debt outstanding?
options: Debt held by the public minus revenues
Debt held by the public plus intragovernmental holdings
Annual deficit plus net interest only
GDP plus federal outlays
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
boss.feedback: Treasury's data dictionary defines total public debt as the sum of the two debt components.

boss.q: Treasury's Debt to the Penny data list debt held by the public separately from intragovernmental holdings. Why?
options: One is a flow and the other is GDP
Intragovernmental holdings represent Treasury debt owned by foreign investors
They are distinct components of total public debt
Debt held by the public is classified as a current federal outlay
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
boss.feedback: The data dictionary separates outside-government holdings from claims held by government accounts.

boss.q: Country A's debt grows 4 percent and nominal GDP grows 7 percent. Country B's debt grows 6 percent and nominal GDP grows 3 percent. Which comparison is correct?
options: A's ratio falls while B's rises
Both debt ratios rise because both nominal debt stocks increase
Both debt ratios fall because nominal GDP increases in both countries
A's debt ratio rises while B's debt ratio falls
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
boss.feedback: A's denominator grows faster than its numerator; B's numerator grows faster than its denominator.

boss.q: A government owes $20 trillion and pays $800 billion in net interest during the year. Which is the stock?
options: The $800 billion interest outlay
Both figures are annual flows
The $20 trillion debt
Neither figure
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
boss.feedback: The debt is outstanding at a date; the interest payment is an annual flow.

boss.q: CBO's February 2026 baseline projects net interest outlays above $1.0 trillion in FY2026, up from $970 billion in FY2025. What is the valid interpretation?
options: Federal debt itself is projected to equal exactly $1.0 trillion
The figures are realized calendar-year revenues collected by Treasury
The annual federal deficit must equal the projected interest outlay
Projected interest outlays rise; neither figure is the debt stock
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
boss.feedback: CBO reports projected fiscal-year interest flows, distinct from the accumulated debt stock.

legendaryBoss.q: CBO’s February 2026 baseline projects debt held by the public at 101 percent of GDP in 2026 and 120 percent in 2036. An analyst claims that nominal debt would therefore rise 19 percent. For that nominal-debt growth claim to be consistent with these displayed ratios, what would nominal GDP have to do?
options: Rise by 19 percent; debt and GDP must grow at the same rate when the ratio increases
Rise by about 0.16 percent; the 19-percentage-point ratio increase is not itself nominal-debt growth
Remain exactly unchanged; subtracting the two ratios gives the percent growth in debt
Fall by about 15.8 percent; a higher debt ratio necessarily implies a smaller economy
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Let GDP growth have factor g. The nominal-debt factor would be (120 / 101)g. Setting it to 1.19 gives g = 1.19(101 / 120) ≈ 1.001583, a 0.16 percent increase. This is a conditional consistency calculation using displayed rounded ratios, not CBO’s GDP projection.

repairQuestions.q: Which measure equals debt held by the public plus intragovernmental holdings?
options: The annual federal deficit
Annual net interest outlays
Federal government purchases
Total public debt outstanding
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
repairQuestions.feedback: Treasury defines total public debt outstanding as the sum of those two components.

repairQuestions.q: Debt is $15 trillion and GDP is $20 trillion. What is debt-to-GDP?
options: 25 percent
35 percent
75 percent
133 percent
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
repairQuestions.feedback: Divide debt by GDP: 15/20 equals 0.75, or 75 percent.

repairQuestions.q: Under a simplifying assumption, debt is $5 trillion and the annual rate is 2 percent. What is the interest cost?
options: $0.1 trillion
$1.0 trillion
$2.5 trillion
$10 trillion
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
repairQuestions.feedback: Two percent of $5 trillion is $0.1 trillion, or $100 billion.

bridgeQuestions.q: Treasury defines debt held by the public as a distinct debt measure. What additional quantity is needed to express that measure relative to the economy?
options: GDP for a matching period
The annual inflation rate alone
Government purchases only
The number of Treasury securities

easy.q: Why is 'a deficit eliminates all private investment' too strong?
options: Crowding out means investment is lower than otherwise, not necessarily zero

Public saving is unrelated to national saving
Investment demand becomes perfectly vertical

easy.q: How can more current investment affect future productive capacity?
options: It can enlarge the stock of physical capital
It must reduce every worker's productivity
It converts all capital into consumption
It eliminates depreciation permanently

easy.feedback: New structures and equipment add to the capital stock and can raise the economy's future capacity, all else equal.

easy.q: Which statement is appropriately qualified?
options: More investment can raise future capacity, all else equal
More investment always guarantees faster growth
Every investment project succeeds equally
Capital accumulation makes saving unnecessary
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment and Capital Formation.
easy.feedback: Investment contributes to capital formation, but outcomes also depend on project quality, depreciation, technology, and other conditions.

easy.q: If private investment is $30 billion lower because of crowding out, what is the careful growth implication?
options: The existing capital stock immediately falls by $30 billion
Capital formation is lower than it otherwise would be
Long-run output must fall by exactly $30 billion
All future economic growth stops
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment and Capital Formation.
easy.feedback: Crowding out reduces the flow of new capital investment relative to the counterfactual; it does not mechanically erase existing capital.

easy.q: Which statement best describes what the investment-to-capital-formation relationship explains?
options: It explains every determinant of productivity
It derives a complete production function
It isolates one channel from investment to productive capacity
It proves convergence across all economies
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment and Capital Formation.
easy.feedback: The relationship isolates how new investment can add to the capital stock; it does not by itself explain every determinant of productivity or growth.

easy.q: A saving increase lowers the real rate and raises investment. What is the next long-run link?
options: More investment must reduce productive capacity
The real rate becomes a capital good
Saving turns directly into current consumption
More investment can add to the future capital stock
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment and Capital Formation.
easy.feedback: The market outcome finances more new capital, which can expand future productive capacity, all else equal.

easy.q: When federal outlays exceed federal revenues during a fiscal year, what is the result?
options: A budget deficit
A budget surplus
A balanced budget
A reduction in gross debt
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
easy.feedback: A deficit occurs because annual outlays are greater than annual revenues.

easy.q: Which fiscal position exists when annual federal revenues exceed annual outlays?
options: A budget deficit
A budget surplus
A balanced budget
A debt rollover
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
easy.feedback: Revenues greater than outlays produce a positive budget balance, called a surplus.

easy.q: Why is federal borrowing not classified as federal revenue in budget accounting?
options: It counts as revenue when interest rates fall
It becomes a transfer payment received by households
It finances a shortfall rather than counting as revenue
It is included in government purchases when debt is issued
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
easy.feedback: Debt issuance supplies financing, but it does not turn the borrowed funds into budget revenue.

easy.q: In the identity public saving = T − G, what must T represent in this accounting framework?
options: Net tax revenue after relevant transfers
Total federal outlays including transfers and net interest
Gross tax collections before subtracting any transfer payments
The accumulated federal debt stock at a specific date
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.

easy.q: Under public saving = T − G, with T defined as net tax revenue and G as government purchases, what does negative public saving mean?
options: Private saving must also be below zero
T is less than G
Nominal GDP must be declining during the year
The government can have no outstanding federal debt
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
easy.feedback: Public saving is negative when net tax revenue T is below government purchases G.

easy.q: A Social Security benefit payment is best classified as what from the federal budget perspective?

Government purchases included in GDP when paid
Intragovernmental holdings of federal debt
A transfer payment within federal outlays
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
easy.feedback: The payment is an outlay that transfers income; it is not a purchase of current output when issued.

easy.q: The federal government buys newly produced rescue equipment. How is the transaction classified?

A transfer payment without a current purchase
Federal revenue
Debt held by the public
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
easy.feedback: Paying for newly produced equipment is both an outlay and government purchases in GDP.

easy.q: Which statement correctly classifies the federal deficit and federal debt?

Deficit: annual flow; debt: accumulated stock

easy.feedback: A deficit is measured over a period, while debt is measured at a point in time.

easy.q: The federal deficit falls from $1.8 trillion to $1.2 trillion. Which conclusion necessarily follows?

The budget moves into surplus
Existing federal debt is eliminated

easy.q: What does a balanced annual federal budget imply about existing federal debt?
options: It immediately reduces the accumulated debt stock to zero
It prevents a new deficit but does not erase existing debt
It proves the preceding fiscal year ended with a surplus
It reclassifies all existing federal debt as current revenue
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
easy.feedback: Balancing annual revenues and outlays addresses the current flow, not the accumulated stock.

easy.q: What generally happens when the federal government runs persistent deficits?

Every annual deficit becomes an equal surplus in a later year
They generally add to accumulated debt
Government purchases are removed from measured GDP during deficit years

easy.feedback: Deficits are recurring gaps that generally require financing and add to the debt stock.

easy.q: Which sequence is correct at an introductory level?

Borrowing, smaller debt, larger surplus by identity
Deficit, financing through borrowing, larger accumulated debt
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
easy.feedback: Borrowing commonly finances a deficit, and repeated borrowing adds to outstanding debt.

easy.q: Which measure covers federal debt held by entities outside the federal government?

The annual federal budget deficit
Debt held by the public
Annual net interest outlays

easy.feedback: Debt held by the public is the portion held outside the federal government under Treasury's definition.

easy.q: What are intragovernmental holdings?

The annual federal deficit
Only Federal Reserve currency
Federal securities held in government accounts
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
easy.feedback: They are claims held within federal government accounts, not debt held by outside investors.

easy.q: Debt held by the public is $24 trillion and nominal GDP is $30 trillion. What is debt-to-GDP?
options: 6 percent
80 percent
24 percent
125 percent
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
easy.feedback: Dividing $24 trillion by $30 trillion and multiplying by 100 gives 80 percent.

easy.q: What does debt held by the public equal to 90 percent of GDP mean?

The annual federal deficit equals 90 percent of nominal GDP
The debt stock equals 90 percent of one year's GDP
The federal government owns 90 percent of domestic production
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
easy.feedback: The ratio compares a debt stock at a date with the scale of annual economic output.

easy.q: Which statement distinguishes federal debt from annual net interest outlays?
options: Debt is a stock; net interest is an annual outlay
Debt and net interest are both annual federal revenue flows
Net interest equals the entire outstanding federal debt stock
Federal debt is a transfer payment measured during each month
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
easy.feedback: Outstanding debt is measured at a date, while net interest is paid over a budget period.

easy.q: Holding the debt stock fixed, what can raise annual interest costs in a simplified example?

A higher average interest rate
A smaller debt stock
A larger budget surplus with no rate change
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
easy.feedback: With the stock held fixed, a higher effective rate raises the interest paid during the year.

Treasury collected a $1.9 trillion surplus
The current federal debt is $1.9 trillion
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Real-World Fiscal-Data Interpretation.
easy.feedback: A baseline published before the fiscal year is complete reports a projection, not a realized result.

easy.q: Treasury's Debt to the Penny dataset reports daily U.S. dollar debt amounts. What does an observation dated August 25, 2026 represent?

A ten-year CBO projection beginning on August 25
A debt stock on August 25, 2026
Federal revenues collected during the month of August
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Real-World Fiscal-Data Interpretation.
easy.feedback: Debt to the Penny records the outstanding debt stock on a specified date; it does not report an annual deficit.

medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.

It remains unchanged
It rises by net taxes
It rises by $25

medium.feedback: Because S = Y − C − G, lower consumption leaves $25 more national saving.

medium.q: A table lists total federal revenues and total outlays including transfers and interest. What does revenues minus outlays measure directly?

The federal budget balance
Private saving Y − T − C
National saving Y − C − G
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
medium.feedback: Total revenues minus total outlays is the budget balance; it should not be relabeled T − G unless the specified components match net taxes and purchases.

medium.q: Private saving falls by $15 while public saving rises by $35. What happens to national saving?

It falls by $20
It rises by $50
It remains unchanged
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
medium.feedback: National saving changes by the sum of component changes: −$15 + $35 = +$20.

Both are $250
Saving is $250 and investment is $900
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
medium.feedback: Y − C − G equals $250; in the closed-economy model both national saving and investment equal that amount.

Neither aggregate changes

140 units
