medium.q: Why does private investment fall after a deficit reduces national saving?
options: The deficit shifts investment demand right
The higher real rate makes fewer projects profitable
The lower real rate discourages borrowing
National saving becomes investment demand
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Government Deficits and Crowding Out.
medium.feedback: Lower supply raises the financing cost, so investment falls along its unchanged downward-sloping demand curve.

medium.q: A budget surplus increases public saving while private saving is unchanged. What follows?
options: National saving falls and crowding out increases
Investment demand shifts left by definition
The real rate must rise
National saving rises and crowding out is reduced
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Government Deficits and Crowding Out.
medium.feedback: Higher public saving raises national saving, shifts supply right, lowers the real rate, and supports more private investment.

medium.q: Why can crowding out matter beyond the current loanable-funds market?
options: Higher rates always destroy the existing capital stock
A deficit makes future production impossible
Lower investment can mean less capital accumulation than otherwise
Public saving becomes identical to depreciation
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment and Capital Formation.
medium.feedback: When financing costs reduce private investment, the future capital stock may grow more slowly than in the counterfactual.

medium.q: Federal revenues are $4.8 trillion and outlays are $6.2 trillion. Using revenues minus outlays, what is the budget balance?
options: +$1.4 trillion
−$11.0 trillion
+$11.0 trillion
−$1.4 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
medium.feedback: Revenues minus outlays equals $4.8 trillion minus $6.2 trillion, or −$1.4 trillion, a deficit.

medium.q: A federal budget balance is reported as +$120 billion. What does the positive sign mean?
options: Revenues exceed outlays by $120 billion
Outlays exceed revenues by $120 billion
Federal debt equals $120 billion
Borrowing increased by exactly $120 billion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
medium.feedback: Under the stated revenues-minus-outlays convention, a positive balance is a surplus.

medium.q: Federal revenues total $5.1 trillion and outlays total $5.9 trillion. What is the deficit expressed as a positive magnitude?
options: −$0.8 trillion
$0.8 trillion
$5.1 trillion
$11.0 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
medium.feedback: Outlays exceed revenues by $0.8 trillion, so the deficit magnitude is reported as positive $0.8 trillion.

medium.q: Net tax revenue T is $3.2 trillion and government purchases G are $3.8 trillion. What is public saving?
options: +$0.6 trillion
$3.2 trillion
−$0.6 trillion
$7.0 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
medium.feedback: Using the stated identity, public saving is T minus G, or $3.2 trillion minus $3.8 trillion.

medium.q: Suppose T is explicitly defined as net tax revenue and equals $2.9 trillion, while government purchases G equal $2.5 trillion. What is public saving?
options: −$0.4 trillion
$2.5 trillion
$5.4 trillion
+$0.4 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
medium.feedback: With the variables defined, T − G equals +$0.4 trillion, indicating positive public saving.

medium.q: Which statement accurately distinguishes mandatory and discretionary spending?
options: Mandatory spending cannot change
Mandatory follows standing law; discretionary depends on appropriations
Discretionary spending has no economically important uses
Every federal transfer payment belongs to discretionary spending
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
medium.feedback: The labels describe budget processes, not whether spending matters or can ever be changed by law.

medium.q: Interest paid on outstanding federal debt belongs in which budget category?
options: Federal revenue from outstanding Treasury securities
A transfer payment counted as government purchases in GDP
Net interest outlays, not government purchases
Intragovernmental holdings in federal trust-fund accounts
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
medium.feedback: Interest outlays service prior borrowing; they are not purchases of newly produced goods and services.

medium.q: Assume a $400 billion deficit is entirely financed by borrowing and there are no other financing adjustments. What happens to federal debt?
options: It falls by $400 billion
It is unchanged
It rises by $400 billion
It becomes exactly $400 billion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
medium.feedback: Under the stated simplifying assumption, borrowing to finance the deficit adds $400 billion to the debt stock.

medium.q: A deficit declines from $900 billion to $500 billion. Has the budget moved into surplus?
options: Yes; the deficit fell by $400 billion
Yes; any deficit reduction is a surplus
No; a surplus is impossible when revenues rise
No; outlays still exceed revenues by $500 billion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
medium.feedback: Reducing a deficit changes its size, but a surplus requires revenues to exceed outlays.

medium.q: Assume there are no other financing adjustments. How can an annual surplus affect federal debt?
options: The surplus can be used to reduce the debt stock
It must increase debt by the surplus amount
It converts debt from a stock into a flow
It leaves debt unchanged by definition
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
medium.feedback: With revenues above outlays, the excess can reduce outstanding borrowing under the stated assumption.

medium.q: Debt is initially $12 trillion. Three annual deficits of $0.4 trillion are fully financed by borrowing, with no other adjustments. What is debt afterward?
options: $13.2 trillion
$10.8 trillion
$12.4 trillion
$14.4 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
medium.feedback: Three deficits add $1.2 trillion to the starting stock under the simplifying assumptions.

medium.q: Why does issuing debt not close a deficit by increasing measured revenue?
options: It counts as mandatory spending in the federal budget
It finances the deficit but is not revenue
It reduces current federal outlays to zero when issued
It represents only borrowing from intragovernmental accounts
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
medium.feedback: Financing explains how the shortfall is covered, not how revenues and outlays are classified.

medium.q: Debt held by the public is $24 trillion and intragovernmental holdings are $6 trillion. What is total public debt outstanding?
options: $30 trillion
$18 trillion
$24 trillion
$144 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
medium.feedback: Treasury defines total public debt outstanding as the sum of the two components.

medium.q: Why is a statement that “federal debt is $X” incomplete?
options: Debt can never be measured in dollars
Different federal debt measures can have different values and meanings
Every debt measure equals the annual deficit
Only GDP can be used to describe debt
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
medium.feedback: The statement should identify whether it means debt held by the public, total public debt, or another specified measure.

medium.q: Two countries each have $2 trillion in public debt. Country A's GDP is $4 trillion; Country B's is $10 trillion. Which has the higher debt-to-GDP ratio?
options: Country B
They have equal ratios
The comparison is impossible even with GDP
Country A
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
medium.feedback: The ratios are 50 percent for A and 20 percent for B, so equal nominal debt implies different relative burdens.

medium.q: Debt grows 5 percent while nominal GDP grows 8 percent. What happens to debt-to-GDP, other things equal?
options: It falls
It rises by 13 percent
It rises because nominal debt rose
It is unchanged
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
medium.feedback: The denominator grows faster than the numerator, so debt becomes a smaller share of GDP.

medium.q: Debt-to-GDP rises from 90 percent to 95 percent. How should the change be stated?
options: An increase of exactly 5 percent
An increase of 5 percentage points
An increase of 95 percentage points
A decrease of 5 percentage points
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
medium.feedback: Subtracting percentage levels gives a five-percentage-point increase; the percent change would be about 5.6 percent.

medium.q: Assume, for illustration, that a $10 trillion debt stock carries a uniform 4 percent annual rate. What is the annual interest cost?
options: $4.0 trillion
$40 trillion
$0.4 trillion
$0.04 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
medium.feedback: Under the explicitly simplified assumption, 4 percent of $10 trillion is $0.4 trillion.

medium.q: Net interest outlays are $0.9 trillion and total outlays are $6.0 trillion. What share of outlays is net interest?
options: 6 percent
9 percent
67 percent
15 percent
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
medium.feedback: Dividing $0.9 trillion by $6.0 trillion gives 0.15, or 15 percent.

medium.q: CBO's February 2026 baseline projects FY2026 revenues of $5.6 trillion and outlays of $7.4 trillion. Using the displayed rounded values, what approximate balance is implied?
options: About a $1.8 trillion surplus
About a $13.0 trillion deficit
A balanced budget
About a $1.8 trillion deficit
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Real-World Fiscal-Data Interpretation.
medium.feedback: The displayed values imply outlays exceed revenues by about $1.8 trillion; CBO separately reports a rounded deficit of $1.9 trillion.

hard.q: Output rises by $100, consumption rises by $70, and government purchases rise by $10. What happens to national saving and loanable-funds supply?
options: National saving rises by $20, so loanable-funds supply shifts right
National saving falls by $20, so loanable-funds supply shifts left
National saving rises by $180, so investment demand shifts right
National saving is unchanged because output and spending all increased
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
hard.feedback: Using S = Y − C − G, the change is +100 − 70 − 10 = +$20. Higher national saving shifts the loanable-funds supply curve right.

hard.q: Net taxes are $320 and government purchases are $280. Private saving then falls by $20 while fiscal quantities remain fixed. What follows?
options: Public saving falls to $20, but national saving remains unchanged
Public saving remains $40, while national saving rises $20 and supply shifts right
Public saving rises to $60, shifting investment demand rather than loanable-funds supply
Public saving stays $40; national saving falls $20
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
hard.feedback: Public saving remains T − G = $40 because fiscal quantities do not change. The $20 decline in private saving therefore lowers national saving and shifts supply left.

hard.q: National saving is initially $420 billion in a closed economy. Improved technology then raises desired investment at every real interest rate. What is the adjustment?
options: Investment stays permanently at $420 billion because the identity prevents demand from shifting
Loanable-funds supply shifts right by exactly the technology improvement, leaving the rate fixed
The identity is violated because desired investment can never differ from saving, even away from equilibrium
Investment demand shifts right, creating upward rate pressure until planned saving and investment are equal again
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
hard.feedback: The accounting identity does not freeze behavior. Higher expected returns shift investment demand right; the real rate adjusts, inducing movements along both curves toward a new equilibrium equality.

hard.q: Government purchases fall by $25 billion in a closed economy with output fixed and the consumption schedule unchanged at each given real rate, while firms also become more optimistic about future sales. Which market description is complete?
options: Only supply shifts right, so both quantity and the real rate must rise
Only investment demand shifts right, so quantity rises and the real rate falls
Both curves shift right; quantity rises and the rate is ambiguous
Both curves shift left, so quantity falls while the real-rate effect is ambiguous
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
hard.feedback: At each given real rate, lower purchases raise planned national saving by $25 billion and shift supply right. Stronger sales expectations shift investment demand right. Both raise equilibrium quantity, but their opposing rate pressures make the rate depend on relative shift magnitudes.

hard.q: Private saving is $360 billion and public saving is −$60 billion. If desired investment at the current real rate is $340 billion, what pressure should move the closed-economy market toward equilibrium?
options: Excess saving puts downward pressure on the real rate, increasing the gap
Excess demand raises the real rate toward equilibrium
Investment demand shifts left automatically by $40 billion because S = I is an identity
Loanable-funds supply shifts right automatically until both quantities equal $360 billion
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
hard.feedback: National saving is $300 billion, below desired investment of $340 billion at the current rate. Excess demand pushes the rate upward, causing movements along the curves toward equilibrium.

hard.q: Refer to the graph above. At a real interest rate above 8 percent, which comparison does the graph imply?

Saving supplied exceeds investment demanded
Saving and investment remain equal
Both curves shift to the right
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.

hard.q: A larger budget deficit lowers public saving while private-saving behavior and investment determinants remain unchanged. Which complete loanable-funds sequence follows?
options: National saving falls, investment demand shifts left, and both the rate and quantity fall
National saving rises, supply shifts right, and investment falls along demand
National saving is unchanged because public saving is not part of loanable-funds supply
Supply shifts left, raising the rate and reducing investment
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
hard.feedback: Public saving is part of national saving, which supplies loanable funds. A deficit lowers that supply, raises the equilibrium real interest rate, and crowds out investment along unchanged demand.

hard.q: The real interest rate is above equilibrium with loanable-funds curves unchanged. Which adjustment moves the market back toward equilibrium?
options: Excess investment demand pushes the rate up, increasing the imbalance
Excess saving pushes the rate down toward equilibrium
Saving supply shifts left until all planned investment disappears
Investment demand shifts right because the high rate makes more projects profitable
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
hard.feedback: Above equilibrium, the quantity of funds supplied exceeds the quantity demanded. Downward pressure on the rate causes movements along both curves until planned saving and investment are equal.

hard.q: Households become more willing to save at every real interest rate. The resulting equilibrium rate falls, and firms undertake more projects. Which description separates the initial cause from the response?
options: Investment demand shifts right first; saving rises through movement along unchanged supply
Both saving supply and investment demand shift right merely because their quantities rise
Saving supply shifts right; investment rises through movement down along unchanged demand
The lower rate shifts saving supply left and shifts investment demand right
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
hard.feedback: Greater willingness to save shifts supply right. The lower equilibrium rate then makes more projects profitable, increasing investment as movement along the original investment-demand curve.

hard.q: A retirement incentive increases saving at every real rate, while improved technology raises expected returns on investment. Which conclusion follows without knowing shift sizes?
options: Only saving supply shifts right, so the real rate must fall
Both curves shift right and equilibrium quantity rises; the real-rate direction is ambiguous
Both curves shift right and the real rate must remain unchanged
Saving supply shifts left while investment demand shifts right, so quantity is ambiguous
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
hard.feedback: The saving incentive shifts supply right, while improved technology shifts investment demand right. Both changes raise equilibrium quantity, but their pressures on the real interest rate oppose one another.

hard.q: Refer to the graph above. The market moves from A to B. Which event is inconsistent with the change shown?
options: Households become more willing to save at every real rate
A new investment tax credit raises expected project profitability
A retirement incentive increases private saving
A budget improvement increases public and national saving
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Changes in Saving.
hard.feedback: The graph shows saving supply shifting right while investment demand remains D0. An investment tax credit would instead shift investment demand right and would not by itself produce this diagram.

National saving falls, shifting supply left; the higher rate lowers investment along demand
Desired investment rises, shifting D0 right; saving supply remains fixed
The lower rate itself shifts saving supply right and investment demand left

hard.feedback: Lower government purchases raise Y − C − G and national saving. Supply shifts from S0 to S1; the lower equilibrium rate then increases investment through movement along D0.

hard.q: Refer to the graph above. From A to B, firms undertake more investment because the real interest rate falls. How should the firm's response be classified?
options: A rightward shift from D0 because every increase in investment is a demand shift
A leftward shift of D0 caused by the lower financing cost
A movement up along S0 caused by improved expected profitability
A movement down along D0 caused by the saving-supply shift

hard.feedback: The initiating change is the rightward saving-supply shift. Firms respond to the lower rate by moving along unchanged investment demand D0, rather than shifting that curve.

hard.q: Refer to the graph above. Can the 20-unit decline in equilibrium quantity be interpreted as the horizontal size of the saving-supply shift?
options: Yes; every change in equilibrium quantity equals the horizontal curve shift
No; quantity also changes through movement along D0
Yes; D0 is fixed, so firms cannot move along it

hard.q: At every given real interest rate, public saving falls by $30 billion while planned private saving rises by $10 billion. With investment demand unchanged, what follows?
options: Supply shifts left, raising the rate and reducing investment
National saving rises $40 billion, shifting supply right and increasing investment
National saving falls $20 billion, shifting investment demand left and lowering the rate
National saving remains unchanged because private saving always offsets a deficit
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Changes in Saving.
hard.feedback: The component changes sum to −$20 billion. Lower national saving shifts loanable-funds supply left, which raises the equilibrium real rate and reduces investment along demand.

hard.q: Refer to the graph above. Both the real interest rate and equilibrium quantity rise from A to B while saving behavior is unchanged. Which diagnosis fits the evidence?
options: Households became more willing to save, shifting loanable-funds supply right
Expected project profitability increased, shifting investment demand right
A larger deficit reduced public saving, shifting loanable-funds supply left
The higher real rate itself shifted investment demand right

options: A tax credit raises expected investment profitability
Households become more willing to save at every real rate
Firms expect weaker future demand for their output
A deficit reduces public saving while investment determinants remain fixed

hard.q: The real interest rate and equilibrium quantity both fall while saving supply is unchanged. Which explanation is most consistent with those observations?
options: Households became more willing to save at every real rate
Weaker expected sales reduced investment demand at every real rate
A larger deficit reduced public and national saving
The lower real rate caused investment demand to shift left
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment Demand.
hard.feedback: With supply fixed, a leftward investment-demand shift lowers both equilibrium variables. Weaker sales expectations provide the causal determinant; the rate change itself produces movement along demand.

hard.q: Refer to the graph above. Saving supply and investment demand both increase. What does theory establish before the graph's marked intersections resolve the remaining issue?
options: The real rate must rise, while quantity is theoretically ambiguous; this graph shows quantity unchanged
Quantity rises; theory leaves the rate ambiguous, but this graph shows no change
Both variables are theoretically ambiguous; the graph shows both falling
Quantity must fall, while the real rate must remain unchanged in every such case
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Simultaneous Shifts.
hard.feedback: Both rightward shifts raise equilibrium quantity. Supply puts downward pressure on the real rate while demand puts upward pressure on it; the marked A and B intersections show those pressures offset here.

The quantity axis fixes the real interest rate whenever quantity increases
The shifts' opposing rate pressures offset in this graph
Both curves are vertical at point B, so neither shift affects the rate

hard.q: A saving incentive raises planned national saving at every real rate, while weaker expected sales reduce desired investment at every real rate. With upward-sloping saving supply and downward-sloping investment demand, which conclusion and information requirement are correct?
options: The real rate falls; investment quantity must fall because only the demand shift affects quantity
The real rate falls; the relative shift magnitudes are needed to determine the investment-quantity change
Investment quantity rises; the relative shift magnitudes are needed to determine the real-rate change
The real rate rises; investment quantity must rise because the saving incentive finances more projects
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Simultaneous Shifts.
hard.feedback: More saving shifts supply right, while weaker sales shift demand left. Both changes lower the real rate. The supply change raises equilibrium quantity and the demand change lowers it, so their relative magnitudes determine the net investment response.

hard.q: Refer to the graph above. A deficit rises by $30 billion while private saving increases by only $10 billion. Which chain matches the movement from A to B?
options: National saving rises $40 billion, supply shifts right, and investment rises along D0
National saving falls $20 billion, D0 shifts left, and the real rate falls
Public and private saving cancel, so neither curve moves from the initial equilibrium
Supply shifts left; the rate rises and investment falls along D0
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Government Deficits and Crowding Out.
hard.feedback: The deficit-driven public-saving loss exceeds the private-saving gain, reducing national saving by $20 billion. The leftward supply shift raises the rate and crowds out investment along unchanged D0.

Any decline in investment quantity requires the demand curve itself to shift
Firms move along D0 after the deficit raises the real rate
The graph shows D0 moving left while saving supply remains fixed
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Government Deficits and Crowding Out.

hard.q: Refer to the graph above. Private saving rises by $30 billion while public saving falls by $10 billion. Which interpretation is consistent with A moving to B?
options: National saving falls $40 billion, shifting supply left and reducing investment
Supply shifts right; the rate falls and investment rises
National saving rises $20 billion, shifting investment demand right and raising the rate
National saving is unchanged because public saving offsets all private-saving changes

Demand shifts left with saving fixed

hard.q: A deficit increases by $30 billion while private saving rises by $10 billion. Which conclusion stays within the loanable-funds mechanism rather than importing multiplier analysis?
options: Aggregate demand must fall by exactly $20 billion after every multiplier effect
Investment demand shifts right by $30 billion because deficits directly raise project profitability
Supply shifts left, raising the rate and crowding out investment
National saving rises $40 billion, so the real rate falls and private investment expands
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Government Deficits and Crowding Out.
hard.feedback: The relevant chain is public saving down, only partly offset by private saving, then national saving and loanable-funds supply down. The task does not calculate short-run aggregate-demand multipliers.

hard.q: Crowding out reduces new machinery purchases, while depreciation and all other growth determinants are unchanged. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: The existing capital stock falls immediately by the full amount of forgone investment
Future output must decline by exactly the reduction in machinery spending
The capital stock is unchanged because investment affects only financial claims
The future capital stock is lower than otherwise, but may still grow
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment and Capital Formation.
hard.feedback: Less gross investment means less addition to the capital stock than in the counterfactual. The stock can still grow if remaining investment exceeds depreciation, so an absolute decline is not implied.

hard.q: One table reports a budget balance of −$900 billion; another describes a deficit of $900 billion. Are the reports consistent?
options: No; both reports must show the shortfall with a negative sign
No; balance and deficit figures cannot have the same magnitude
Yes; one is signed and the other gives the deficit magnitude
Yes; both figures describe a $900 billion budget surplus
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
hard.feedback: A negative revenues-minus-outlays balance and a positive deficit magnitude can describe the same shortfall.

hard.q: Revenues rise from $4.9 trillion to $5.2 trillion while outlays rise from $6.0 trillion to $6.1 trillion. How does the budget balance change?
options: It worsens by $0.2 trillion
It improves by $0.3 trillion and becomes a budget surplus
It remains unchanged as both rise
It improves by $0.2 trillion but remains negative
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
hard.feedback: The balance moves from −$1.1 trillion to −$0.9 trillion, an improvement of $0.2 trillion.

hard.q: A table gives total federal revenues of $5 trillion and total outlays, including transfers and interest, of $6 trillion. What should revenues minus outlays be called?
options: A $1 trillion federal budget deficit
Public saving of −$1 trillion under T − G
Private saving of $1 trillion
Government purchases of $6 trillion
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
hard.feedback: Total revenues minus total outlays is the budget balance. In the T − G public-saving shorthand, T must be net tax revenue and G must be government purchases.

hard.q: Holding the relevant definitions and other items fixed, what is the basic public-saving implication of a larger budget deficit?
options: Public saving is necessarily higher
Public saving is lower
Private saving becomes zero by identity
Government purchases are no longer part of GDP
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
hard.feedback: A wider fiscal shortfall reduces the government's contribution to national saving under the introductory accounting link.

hard.q: A benefit payment and a purchase of new federal vehicles are both outlays. What distinguishes their GDP treatment?
options: Both enter G
Neither enters GDP
Only the benefit payment enters G directly when Treasury pays it
Only the vehicle purchase enters G when paid
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
hard.feedback: A transfer redistributes income, whereas the vehicle purchase pays for current production.

hard.q: Taxes raise $4.7 trillion and borrowing supplies $1.1 trillion. Which amount is federal revenue?
options: $4.7 trillion
$1.1 trillion
$5.8 trillion
Neither amount
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
hard.feedback: Taxes are receipts; borrowing finances the gap and is not recorded as revenue.

hard.q: Debt begins at $18.0 trillion. Deficits of $0.8 trillion and $0.5 trillion follow in two years. Assuming borrowing finances each deficit and no other adjustments occur, what is debt after year two?
options: $17.7 trillion
$19.3 trillion
$18.5 trillion
$20.6 trillion
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
hard.feedback: The two deficits add $1.3 trillion to the initial $18.0 trillion debt stock.

hard.q: A report says debt reached $25 trillion while the year's deficit was $1 trillion. Why are the figures not contradictory?
options: The annual deficit excludes most categories of federal outlays
Debt measures only interest payments
Debt is a stock; the deficit is an annual flow
Debt and deficit figures must become equal after each fiscal year
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
hard.feedback: The annual deficit is one contributor to the much larger accumulated debt stock.

hard.q: Why is the reported annual deficit not always identical to the measured change in federal debt?
options: Reported deficits do not require financing through any source
Federal debt is measured only at ten-year intervals
Annual deficit calculations exclude all categories of federal revenue
Financing adjustments can separate the debt change from the deficit
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
hard.feedback: Real Treasury financing includes adjustments beyond the simplified classroom assumption that all deficit financing maps one-for-one into debt.

hard.q: A government raises purchases with net taxes unchanged. Private-saving behavior is unchanged. Which sequence describes the fiscal consequence?
options: Private saving falls but public saving is unchanged, because government purchases are household consumption
Public saving rises and the budget moves toward surplus, reducing the need to issue government debt
Public saving falls and the budget moves toward deficit, increasing borrowing needs if the shortfall is debt-financed
Public saving falls but issuing debt counts as revenue, so borrowing restores the budget balance
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
hard.feedback: With net taxes unchanged, higher government purchases reduce public saving T − G and move the budget toward deficit. Borrowing can finance the shortfall, but debt issuance does not count as revenue or reverse the decline in public saving.

hard.q: Which statement about sustained government borrowing is appropriately conditional?
options: It always eliminates all private investment
It can leave broader financial conditions permanently unaffected in every case
It can guarantee faster economic growth whenever the government borrows
It can raise rates and reduce some private investment
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
hard.feedback: The possible effect depends on economic conditions; it is not an unconditional outcome.

hard.q: A report lists debt held by the public at $25 trillion and total public debt outstanding at $32 trillion. What can be inferred?
options: The $7 trillion difference is the annual deficit
The two figures must refer to different countries
The difference reflects intragovernmental holdings under the stated Treasury definitions
Debt held by the public includes all intragovernmental holdings
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
hard.feedback: Total public debt combines debt held by the public with intragovernmental holdings.

hard.q: Why should debt subject to the statutory limit not automatically be substituted for debt held by the public?
options: The debt limit is an annual flow
Debt held by the public excludes every type of Treasury security
Both measures are identical
The measures cover different sets of federal obligations
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
hard.feedback: Debt measures have distinct legal and analytical boundaries, so the label must match the source.

hard.q: Debt rises from $20 trillion to $21 trillion while nominal GDP rises from $20 trillion to $22 trillion. What happens to debt-to-GDP?
options: It rises from 100 percent to 105 percent because debt increases
It remains at 100 percent
It falls from 100 percent to about 95.5 percent
It falls from 100 percent to approximately 50 percent
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
hard.feedback: Debt grows 5 percent, but GDP grows 10 percent, reducing the ratio to approximately 21/22.

hard.q: Economy A has $9 trillion in debt and $12 trillion in GDP. Economy B has $12 trillion in debt and $24 trillion in GDP. Which has the higher debt-to-GDP ratio?
options: Economy B
They are equal
Nominal debt alone makes comparison impossible after GDP is supplied
Economy A
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
hard.feedback: A's ratio is 75 percent, compared with 50 percent for B.

hard.q: Nominal debt rises, yet debt-to-GDP falls. What must be true under the stated comparison?
options: Nominal GDP grew faster than debt
GDP necessarily fell
The annual federal budget necessarily recorded a surplus
Part of the federal debt was reclassified as current revenue
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
hard.feedback: A falling ratio with a rising numerator requires the denominator to grow at a faster proportional rate.

hard.q: Why can rising interest outlays contribute to future deficits, other things equal?
options: They raise outlays without purchasing current services
They can raise tax revenue by the same amount
They reduce the outstanding debt stock as soon as interest is paid
They are excluded from total outlays in federal budget accounting
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
hard.feedback: Higher interest costs widen the gap between revenues and outlays unless offset elsewhere.

hard.q: CBO's February 2026 baseline projects the deficit at 5.8 percent of GDP in 2026 and 6.7 percent in 2036. What is the change?
options: An increase of 0.9 percentage point
An increase of 0.9 percent
An increase of 12.5 percentage points
A decrease of 0.9 percentage point
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Real-World Fiscal-Data Interpretation.
hard.feedback: Subtracting the two projected shares gives 0.9 percentage point.

elite.q: Households reduce current consumption and buy a firm's newly issued bonds. The firm uses the proceeds for new machinery and to purchase an existing office building. Which chain is economically correct?
options: Both firm purchases are current GDP investment because both use borrowed funds
The bond purchase is physical investment, while neither firm purchase enters GDP
Household saving enters GDP directly, and the machinery is only a financial asset
Saving finances the firm, but only the new machinery is current GDP investment
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
elite.feedback: The bond market channels household saving to the borrower. New machinery is current production and GDP investment; transferring an existing building is not new production.

elite.q: At every given real interest rate, planned private saving increases by $25 billion, but a larger deficit reduces public saving by $40 billion. With investment demand unchanged, which sequence follows?
options: National saving rises by $65 billion; supply shifts right, the real rate falls, and investment rises
National saving falls by $15 billion; supply shifts left, the real rate rises, and investment falls
National saving falls by $15 billion; investment demand shifts left, lowering both rate and quantity
National saving rises by $15 billion; supply shifts right, but investment necessarily falls
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
elite.feedback: The public-saving decline is larger than the private-saving increase, so national saving falls by $15 billion. Supply shifts left, raising financing costs and crowding out investment along demand.

elite.q: In a closed economy, at every given real interest rate, planned private saving rises by $20 billion while public saving falls by $35 billion. At the same time, new technology raises desired investment. What can be concluded without knowing the investment-demand shift magnitude?
options: Both curves shift right; quantity rises, while the real rate is ambiguous
Supply shifts left only; both the real rate and quantity must fall
Investment demand shifts right only; the real rate rises and quantity must rise
Supply shifts left, demand shifts right; the rate rises and quantity is ambiguous
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
elite.feedback: At each given real rate, planned national saving falls by $15 billion, shifting supply left. Technology shifts investment demand right. Both shifts raise the real rate, but their quantity effects oppose one another; the final change in realized saving and investment is therefore not fixed at −$15 billion.

elite.q: Refer to the graph above. Treat the displayed curves as straight lines. At a temporary real interest rate of 10 percent, how large is the planned imbalance, and what adjustment returns this market toward A?
options: A 40-unit excess supply; a falling rate shifts both curves toward A
An 80-unit excess supply; a falling rate reduces saving supplied and increases investment demanded
An 80-unit excess demand; a rising rate reduces investment demanded and increases saving supplied
A 40-unit excess demand; a rising rate shifts saving supply right
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
elite.feedback: At 10 percent, S0 supplies 180 units and D0 demands 100, leaving excess supply of 80. A lower rate moves down along S0 and D0 toward their intersection at 140 units and 8 percent; neither curve must shift.

elite.q: A higher real return encourages households to postpone consumption, while a new retirement incentive increases saving at every real rate. How should these effects be represented?
options: Both changes shift saving supply right because each raises observed saving
Movement along supply, followed by a rightward supply shift
The higher rate shifts supply right, while the incentive causes movement along the curve
Both changes cause movement along the original saving curve because neither affects demand
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
elite.feedback: The current real rate determines a quantity supplied on a given curve. A retirement incentive changes saving behavior at every real rate, so it shifts the whole curve.

elite.q: A saving incentive shifts loanable-funds supply right. The lower equilibrium real rate makes more investment projects profitable, and firms also become more optimistic about future sales. Which description is complete?
options: Both investment increases are movements along demand because firms ultimately borrow more
Both investment increases shift demand because the equilibrium rate changes
The saving incentive shifts investment demand right, while optimism moves firms along that curve
Movement along demand, followed by a separate rightward demand shift
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
elite.feedback: The saving shock lowers the rate and causes movement along the existing investment-demand curve. Optimism changes desired investment at every rate, so it separately shifts demand right.

elite.q: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion, and the lines are straight. A fiscal change lowers public saving by $55 billion at every real rate, while a separate incentive raises planned private saving by $15 billion at every rate. Investment demand does not shift. Which comparison correctly connects the policy shifts with A and B?
options: Saving supply shifts left by $20 billion, and equilibrium investment falls by $40 billion
Saving supply shifts left by $40 billion, but equilibrium investment falls by $20 billion
Saving supply shifts left by $70 billion, but equilibrium investment falls by $20 billion
Saving supply shifts left by $40 billion, and equilibrium investment falls by $40 billion
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Changes in Saving.
elite.feedback: At any given rate, the saving-supply change is −55 + 15 = −$40 billion, matching the horizontal distance between S0 and S1. The marked equilibria move from 100 to 80, so investment falls by $20 billion. The higher rate partly offsets the supply reduction by inducing additional saving along the shifted schedule.

elite.q: Refer to the graph above. Improved technology raises investment demand, while households also become more willing to save. What limitation matters when using this graph for that scenario?
options: It depicts the saving shift but keeps investment demand fixed
It depicts both shifts and therefore proves the real rate must rise
It cannot show investment demand because D1 is a saving curve
It omits the household-saving supply shift

elite.feedback: The graph cleanly represents technology through D0 shifting to D1. The scenario also requires saving supply to shift right, but S0 remains fixed, so the full combined outcome is not shown.

elite.q: Technology improves expected project returns, but the equilibrium real interest rate subsequently rises. Which statement correctly separates the two effects on investment?
options: Technology moves firms along demand, while the higher rate shifts the entire curve left
Both changes shift demand right because equilibrium investment initially rises
The higher rate shifts loanable-funds supply left and leaves investment demand unchanged
Demand shifts right; the higher rate partly offsets the increase
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment Demand.
elite.feedback: Improved technology changes profitability at every rate and shifts investment demand right. The endogenous rate increase makes fewer marginal projects profitable along the new curve, partly offsetting the initial increase.

elite.q: Refer to the graph above. In general, simultaneous rightward shifts make the real-rate effect ambiguous. What does this particular outcome imply about the depicted shift magnitudes?
options: The saving shift is absent because the real rate did not fall
The investment-demand shift dominates, so the real rate must rise above 6 percent
Both shifts reduce quantity, but equal magnitudes conceal the decline
The rate pressures offset while both shifts raise quantity
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Simultaneous Shifts.
elite.feedback: A rightward supply shift pushes the rate down and a rightward demand shift pushes it up. The unchanged 6 percent rate shows offsetting rate effects, while both shifts raise quantity from A to B.

elite.q: A deficit lowers saving while new technology raises investment demand. What can be concluded without shift magnitudes?
options: The real rate falls; quantity rises
Both outcomes fall
Both outcomes are necessarily unchanged
The real rate rises; the quantity effect is ambiguous
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Simultaneous Shifts.
elite.feedback: Supply left and demand right both raise the rate, but they push equilibrium quantity in opposite directions.

elite.q: Refer to the graph above. A budget improvement raises public saving by $25 billion while private saving falls by $10 billion. What connects the accounting to the new equilibrium?
options: National saving falls $35 billion, shifting supply left; the higher rate reduces investment
National saving rises $15 billion, shifting D0 right; the real rate and quantity both rise
National saving remains fixed, so the move to B must come from weaker investment demand
National saving rises, shifting supply right and increasing investment along D0
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Government Deficits and Crowding Out.
elite.feedback: Public and private saving changes sum to +$15 billion. The resulting supply increase matches S0 to S1; the lower rate then raises investment through movement along D0.
elite.imageAlt: Loanable-funds graph with S0, S1, D0 and labeled intersections A and B.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is labeled Quantity of loanable funds; the vertical axis is labeled Real interest rate. Coordinates below are (quantity, rate). The quantity axis has no currency scale. All curves are straight. The solid red line labeled S0 slopes upward through (0, 5) and (60, 8). The dashed red line labeled S1 slopes upward through (0, 1) and (100, 6). The solid blue line labeled D0 slopes downward through (0, 11) and (220, 0). Point A marks the S0–D0 intersection at (60, 8). Point B marks the S1–D0 intersection at (100, 6). A numbered grid provides the coordinate scale.

elite.q: A published table rounds revenues to $5.6 trillion, outlays to $7.4 trillion, and the deficit to $1.9 trillion. Why need the rounded entries not subtract exactly?
options: The displayed figures were rounded independently
The deficit excludes displayed revenues
Borrowing is added to both displayed revenues and displayed outlays
The deficit uses calendar-year data
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
elite.feedback: Independent rounding can make displayed components differ slightly from an identity calculated with unrounded values.

elite.q: A budget worksheet reports $920 billion of cash inflows, including $180 billion from issuing new debt, and $870 billion of total outlays. All remaining inflows are revenues; there are no other financing adjustments. What are the budget balance and the amount of new borrowing left to increase cash balances?
options: A $50 billion surplus and no borrowing needed for the outlays
A $130 billion deficit and a $50 billion cash increase
A $130 billion deficit and a $180 billion cash increase
A $310 billion deficit and a $130 billion cash decrease
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
elite.feedback: Revenues exclude borrowing: 920 − 180 = $740 billion. Revenues minus outlays equal 740 − 870 = −$130 billion. Of the $180 billion borrowed, $130 billion finances the deficit and $50 billion increases cash balances.

elite.q: A simplified fiscal account reports gross tax receipts of $900 billion, transfers of $180 billion, government purchases of $660 billion and interest payments of $70 billion. These are all revenues and outlays. For this exercise define T as gross taxes minus transfers, excluding interest. Which pair gives textbook public saving T − G and the full budget balance?
options: Public saving is $240 billion; the full budget has a $60 billion surplus
Public saving is −$10 billion; the full budget also has a $10 billion deficit
Public saving is $60 billion; the full budget has a $10 billion deficit
Public saving is $60 billion; the full budget has a $60 billion surplus
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
elite.feedback: Under the stated convention, T = 900 − 180 = $720 billion and T − G = $60 billion. Total outlays are 180 + 660 + 70 = $910 billion, giving a $10 billion deficit. The $70 billion difference is interest, which this exercise excludes from net taxes. Transfers are already deducted in T and must not be deducted a second time.

elite.q: A speaker calls all discretionary outlays “optional” and all mandatory outlays “uncontrollable.” What is wrong with the claim?
options: Discretionary outlays are made without any congressional appropriations
The labels describe funding rules, not permanence or importance
Mandatory programs never transfer
Net interest outlays are classified as federal budget revenues
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
elite.feedback: Process labels do not settle importance, desirability, or whether future law can alter spending.

elite.q: A deficit falls from $1.4 trillion to $0.9 trillion while debt rises. Which explanation is coherent?
options: Debt can still rise because the budget remains in deficit
A smaller deficit is a surplus
Debt can rise only when the annual deficit also becomes larger
Debt rose because revenues exceeded outlays
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
elite.feedback: A reduced deficit remains positive borrowing need; it need not reverse the direction of the debt stock.

elite.q: A proposal balances the budget beginning next year. Which claim goes beyond what that fact establishes?
options: No new deficit is planned next year
The existing federal debt will disappear next year
Projected revenues equal projected outlays next year
The annual budget position would improve if it was previously in deficit
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
elite.feedback: A balanced flow prevents new deficit accumulation but does not repay the accumulated stock immediately.

elite.q: Two releases report different debt values on the same date, but one labels debt held by the public and the other labels total public debt outstanding. What is the best conclusion?
options: The releases use different debt measures
One release must be false
The numerical difference must equal the deficit recorded on that date
The smaller reported figure must represent intragovernmental holdings alone
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
elite.feedback: Measure definitions must be aligned before interpreting a numerical difference.

elite.q: A commentator says Economy B is in the weaker fiscal position because its nominal debt is larger than Economy A's. What evidence is missing?
options: The unemployment rate alone
Comparable GDP and consistently defined debt
Only the total number of public and private bondholders
A complete list of every government agency in both economies
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
elite.feedback: Relative comparisons require both economic scale and consistently defined debt measures.

elite.q: In a simplified debt portfolio, $600 billion remains at a fixed 2 percent annual rate and $400 billion is refinanced from 2 to 5 percent at the start of the year. Principal stays constant; rates apply for the full year and there are no interest receipts. Revenues and noninterest outlays are unchanged. How do interest outlays and the deficit change?
options: Interest outlays become $50 billion and the deficit widens $30 billion
Interest outlays become $32 billion and the deficit widens $12 billion
Interest outlays become $20 billion and the deficit is unchanged
Interest outlays become $32 billion and the deficit widens $32 billion
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
elite.feedback: Initial interest is (600 + 400)(0.02) = $20 billion. New interest is 600(0.02) + 400(0.05) = 12 + 20 = $32 billion. The $12 billion increase widens the deficit by the same amount. The current refinancing rate applies only to the repriced portion, not the whole portfolio.

elite.q: What does CBO's February 2026 baseline projection establish about the future?
options: Fixed future legislation
A conditional benchmark, not a guaranteed forecast
Realized Treasury budget results for every year in the projection window
A projection that eliminates uncertainty about future interest rates
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Real-World Fiscal-Data Interpretation.
elite.feedback: Baseline projections are conditional benchmarks whose outcomes can change with laws, economic conditions, and other developments.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion. The straight S0 and S1 curves capture a fiscal change, with the private-saving schedule unchanged and D0 fixed. Starting from B, a second policy raises planned private saving by $15 billion at every real rate. How much must public saving rise from its level at B to restore A?
options: $40 billion; the private-saving incentive cannot change national saving
$5 billion; the required saving shift equals the 20-unit equilibrium-quantity gap
$55 billion; the private-saving increase must be added to the original supply shortfall
$25 billion; together the two changes restore the original saving schedule
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Changes in Saving.
legendary.feedback: At any given rate, S1 lies 40 units left of S0. Restoring S0 therefore requires $40 billion of additional planned national saving, not merely the 20-unit difference in equilibrium quantity. Private saving supplies $15 billion of that shift, leaving $25 billion of public saving. With D0 fixed, restoring S0 restores A.
legendary.imageAlt: Loanable-funds graph with S0, S1, D0 and labeled intersections A and B.

The quantity axis has no currency scale. All curves are straight. The solid red line labeled S0 slopes upward through (0, 2) and (100, 7). The dashed red line labeled S1 slopes upward through (0, 4) and (80, 8). The solid blue line labeled D0 slopes downward through (0, 12) and (240, 0). Point A marks the S0–D0 intersection at (100, 7). Point B marks the S1–D0 intersection at (80, 8). A numbered grid provides the coordinate scale.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph above. Technology raises investment demand, but a new deficit simultaneously reduces national saving. Which conclusion goes beyond what this graph establishes?
options: Technology places upward pressure on the real interest rate
That the combined scenario must raise equilibrium quantity from 80 to 120
The deficit would shift loanable-funds supply left
The two shocks together place upward pressure on the real interest rate
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment Demand.
legendary.feedback: This graph isolates a rightward demand shift with supply fixed. Adding a deficit would shift supply left; both shocks raise the rate, but their quantity effects oppose one another, so 120 is not guaranteed.
legendary.imageAlt: Loanable-funds graph with S0, D0, D1 and labeled intersections A and B.

The quantity axis has no currency scale. All curves are straight. The solid red line labeled S0 slopes upward through (0, 1) and (80, 5). Point A marks the S0–D0 intersection at (80, 5). Point B marks the S0–D1 intersection at (120, 7). A numbered grid provides the coordinate scale.

legendary.q: Expected investment profitability falls while a budget deficit also reduces national saving. What must happen, and what remains uncertain?
options: The real rate falls, while equilibrium quantity is ambiguous
Quantity falls; the real-rate direction is ambiguous
Both the real rate and quantity must rise
The real rate must remain unchanged, while quantity falls
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment Demand.
legendary.feedback: Investment demand shifts left and loanable-funds supply shifts left. Both changes reduce equilibrium quantity, but demand puts downward pressure on the rate while supply puts upward pressure on it.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion, and the straight-line shifts summarize all changes in saving and investment behavior. Public saving falls by $10 billion at every real rate, while technology raises investment demand. What private-saving shift is required to reconcile the graph with that fiscal change?
options: A $30 billion increase at every rate; subtracting the public-saving decline gives the $40 billion supply increase
A $50 billion increase at every rate; net saving supply and investment demand each move right by $40 billion
A $10 billion increase at every rate; an unchanged interest rate means national saving is unchanged
A $40 billion increase at every rate; public saving is excluded when constructing the saving-supply curve
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Simultaneous Shifts.
legendary.feedback: At 6 percent, S0 and D0 each have quantity 40, while S1 and D1 each have quantity 80. Each schedule shifts right by $40 billion. Since national saving combines private and public saving, the private shift must satisfy private change − 10 = 40, giving +$50 billion. The two shifts leave the depicted equilibrium rate at 6 percent.

legendary.loanableFundsScenario: Saving and investment demand both increase

legendary.q: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion, and the curves are straight. A budget improvement shifts S0 to S1; the private-saving schedule and investment demand are unchanged. What does the graph imply about the rise in public saving and the induced change in private saving between A and B?
options: Public saving rises $40 billion; private saving is unchanged because its schedule is fixed
Public saving rises $80 billion; private saving falls $40 billion as the rate declines
Public saving rises $80 billion; private saving rises $40 billion as investment expands
Public saving rises $40 billion; private saving falls $80 billion because D0 does not shift
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Government Deficits and Crowding Out.
legendary.feedback: The horizontal supply shift is 80 units: at an 8 percent rate S0 is at 60 and S1 is at 140. With the private-saving schedule unchanged, that shift is the $80 billion public-saving increase. Final national saving and investment rise only from 60 to 100, or $40 billion. Private saving consequently changes by 40 − 80 = −$40 billion through movement along its schedule as the rate falls.
