Point B marks the S1–D0 intersection at (100, 6). A numbered grid provides the coordinate scale.

legendary.q: National saving rises and lowers the real interest rate, but many funded projects have low returns and depreciation is unusually high. What is the careful long-run conclusion?
options: The higher saving rate guarantees an equal permanent increase in productive capacity
More financing can support capital formation, but does not guarantee it
Every financed project becomes physical capital, so project quality and depreciation are irrelevant
Greater saving must reduce investment because the closed-economy identity fixes the capital stock
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment and Capital Formation.
legendary.feedback: Greater saving can lower financing costs and enable more investment. Actual capital accumulation and future output still depend on project quality, depreciation, technology, and other conditions.

legendary.q: A government starts the year with $3,600 billion of debt. Revenues are $760 billion and outlays are $940 billion. It issues $500 billion of debt, including debt used to repay $270 billion of maturing principal; remaining financing may change cash balances. With no other debt or financing adjustments, which reconciliation is correct?
options: A $180 billion deficit, ending debt of $4,100 billion, and a $320 billion increase in cash
A $320 billion surplus, ending debt of $3,830 billion, and a $50 billion increase in cash
A $180 billion deficit, ending debt of $3,830 billion, and a $50 billion increase in cash
A $450 billion deficit, ending debt of $3,780 billion, and unchanged cash
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
legendary.feedback: The deficit is 940 − 760 = $180 billion; debt issuance is financing, not revenue. Net issuance is 500 − 270 = $230 billion, so ending debt is $3,830 billion. Net financing exceeds the deficit by $50 billion, increasing cash. Principal repayment is not counted again as a budget outlay.

legendary.q: The deficit becomes smaller, nominal debt rises, and debt-to-GDP falls. Which combination can explain all three facts?
options: A surplus raises debt
Debt falls faster than GDP while the annual deficit becomes larger
Debt rises, but nominal GDP grows faster
A balanced budget erases existing debt while nominal GDP remains unchanged
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
legendary.feedback: The deficit can still add to nominal debt, while faster GDP growth lowers the debt ratio.

legendary.q: At year-end a government owes $2,400 billion. During the final month its deficit was $20 billion. An analyst divides 2,400 by 20 and calls the result a 120 percent annual debt-growth rate. If the monthly deficit instead remained constant for a full future year, all deficits were borrowed, and no other debt adjustments occurred, what would the calculation establish?
options: The original quotient is a 120 percent growth rate; annualizing the deficit leaves that rate unchanged
The original quotient is 120 years of deficits; the stated future scenario implies 1 percent annual debt growth
The original quotient is a 10 percent growth rate; dividing it by 12 gives annual debt growth
The original quotient is 120 months of deficits; the stated future scenario implies 10 percent annual debt growth
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
legendary.feedback: A stock of $2,400 billion divided by a flow of $20 billion per month gives 120 months, not a percent growth rate. Under the explicit future assumption, twelve monthly deficits add $240 billion to debt; 240 / 2,400 = 10 percent. One observed month alone does not establish that future path.

legendary.q: Two packages require the same additional borrowing, leave public saving equally lower, and face the same unchanged private-saving and investment-demand schedules. Package A finances productive public infrastructure; Package B finances transfers. What evidence is needed to decide whether A leaves more total productive capital than before the policy?
options: Whether the public-capital addition exceeds the private-capital formation displaced by the higher real rate
Whether A issues less debt than B, even though their additional borrowing is stated to be equal
Whether transfers count as current public-capital formation at the moment they are paid
Whether a decline in public saving is itself a one-for-one measure of lost private capital
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
legendary.feedback: Both packages create the same initial loanable-funds pressure under the stated schedules. A also adds public productive capital. Its net capital effect depends on that addition relative to displaced private capital formation; borrowing alone does not establish the sign. No project-valuation or AD-AS model is needed for this comparison.

legendary.q: A government begins with debt equal to 80 percent of nominal GDP. During the year it borrows an amount equal to 4 percent of initial GDP to finance its deficit, with no other debt adjustments. Nominal GDP grows 8 percent. Which result reconciles the deficit, the debt stock and the debt ratio?
options: Debt rises 4 percent, and debt-to-GDP falls to exactly 76 percent
Debt falls 4 percent, so debt-to-GDP falls to about 77.8 percent
Debt rises 5 percent, but debt-to-GDP falls to about 77.8 percent
Debt rises 5 percent, so debt-to-GDP rises to 84 percent
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
legendary.feedback: Normalize initial GDP to 100: debt starts at 80, borrowing adds 4 and GDP rises to 108. Debt growth is 4 / 80 = 5 percent; the new ratio is 84 / 108 ≈ 77.8 percent. Faster denominator growth lowers the ratio despite the borrowing-financed deficit.

legendary.q: Debt-to-GDP rises from 80 percent to 88 percent while nominal GDP rises 5 percent. The debt measure and accounting dates are comparable. Which comparison correctly separates the ratio change from the change in nominal debt?
options: The ratio rises 8 percentage points, or 10 percent; nominal debt rises 10 percent
The ratio rises 8 percent, or 10 percentage points; nominal debt rises 13 percent
The ratio rises 8 percentage points, or 10 percent; nominal debt rises 5 percent
The ratio rises 8 percentage points, or 10 percent; nominal debt rises 15.5 percent
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
legendary.feedback: The ratio increases by 8 points and by 8 / 80 = 10 percent relative to its initial level. Nominal debt changes by the ratio factor times the GDP factor: (88 / 80)(1.05) = 1.155, or 15.5 percent. The ratio growth rate is not the numerator growth rate when GDP also changes.

legendary.q: A Treasury observation reports total public debt outstanding, while a CBO projection reports debt held by the public as a percentage of GDP. What must be aligned before comparing them?
options: Only the agency names
Only whether both reported fiscal values have positive signs
Definition, date, status, and units
Nothing, because all federal debt measures and dates are interchangeable
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Real-World Fiscal-Data Interpretation.
legendary.feedback: A sound comparison requires the same measure, date/status, and units.

legendary.q: CBO’s February 2026 baseline gives projected debt-held-by-the-public ratios of 101 percent of GDP in 2026 and 120 percent in 2036. Using only these displayed ratios, when would nominal debt in 2036 exceed nominal debt in 2026?
options: When nominal GDP in 2036 exceeds 120 percent of its 2026 level; a smaller GDP increase implies falling debt
Only when nominal GDP is unchanged; otherwise the two debt ratios cannot be compared
For every possible positive GDP level in 2036; a higher ratio proves a larger nominal debt stock
When nominal GDP in 2036 exceeds about 84.2 percent of its 2026 level; the ratios alone do not establish GDP’s change
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Real-World Fiscal-Data Interpretation.
legendary.feedback: Debt is its GDP share times nominal GDP. Thus 1.20 × GDP2036 must exceed 1.01 × GDP2026, requiring GDP2036 / GDP2026 > 101 / 120 ≈ 0.8417. A higher ratio alone does not identify nominal-debt growth without denominator evidence. This threshold uses the displayed rounded ratios and is not a forecast of GDP.

easyBoss.q: Which action is saving in the macroeconomic sense?
options: Setting aside current income for future use
Buying newly produced factory equipment
Building a newly constructed apartment
Adding unsold goods to business inventories
easyBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
easyBoss.feedback: Saving is current income not used for consumption; the other choices are forms of new macroeconomic investment.

easyBoss.q: Why does construction of a new home count as investment in GDP?
options: It creates a new long-lived residential asset
Every household purchase is classified as investment
The buyer must have purchased an existing stock
Residential services are excluded from production
easyBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
easyBoss.feedback: GDP conventions treat new residential construction as investment because it adds a durable structure that yields housing services.

easyBoss.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes financial investment from macroeconomic investment?
options: Financial assets can change ownership without creating new capital
Every financial-asset trade adds equally to current GDP investment
Macroeconomic investment means purchasing only stocks and bonds
New equipment is saving rather than macroeconomic investment
easyBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
easyBoss.feedback: Trading an existing claim need not add to current production, while new equipment, structures, inventories, and qualifying intellectual property do.

easyBoss.q: Which institution is acting as a financial intermediary?
options: A bank accepts deposits and makes business loans
A factory converts steel into new machinery
A retailer sells newly produced consumer goods
A household consumes services from an existing home
easyBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
easyBoss.feedback: A financial intermediary gathers funds from savers and supplies financing to borrowers rather than producing the capital good itself.

easyBoss.q: Which expression gives national saving in the stated closed-economy accounting model?
options: Y − T − C
T − G
Y − C − G
C + I + G
easyBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
easyBoss.feedback: Adding private saving Y − T − C and public saving T − G cancels T, leaving Y − C − G.

easyBoss.q: Income is $1,200, consumption is $760, and government purchases are $260. What is national saving?
easyBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
easyBoss.feedback: National saving equals Y − C − G, so $1,200 − $760 − $260 = $180.

easyBoss.q: Annual federal revenues equal $5.0 trillion and outlays equal $5.3 trillion. Which fiscal position is shown?
options: A $0.3 trillion surplus
A balanced budget
A $5.3 trillion debt stock
A $0.3 trillion deficit
easyBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
easyBoss.feedback: Outlays exceed revenues by $0.3 trillion, so the annual budget is in deficit.

easyBoss.q: With T defined as net tax revenue and G as government purchases, T equals $800 billion and G equals $900 billion. What is public saving?
options: +$100 billion
$800 billion
$1.7 trillion
−$100 billion
easyBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
easyBoss.feedback: T − G equals −$100 billion, so public saving is negative.

easyBoss.q: Which expression gives the broad Treasury relationship for total public debt outstanding?
options: Debt held by the public minus revenues
Debt held by the public plus intragovernmental holdings
Annual deficit plus net interest only
GDP plus federal outlays
easyBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
easyBoss.feedback: Treasury's data dictionary defines total public debt as the sum of the two debt components.

easyBoss.q: A government owes $20 trillion and pays $800 billion in net interest during the year. Which is the stock?
options: The $800 billion interest outlay
Both figures are annual flows
The $20 trillion debt
Neither figure
easyBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
easyBoss.feedback: The debt is outstanding at a date; the interest payment is an annual flow.

mediumBoss.q: Which purchase is counted as new macroeconomic investment in GDP?
options: A household buys an existing corporate share
A firm buys newly produced machinery
An investor buys an existing government bond
A collector buys a previously owned painting
mediumBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
mediumBoss.feedback: New production equipment expands the capital stock and is GDP investment; secondary financial and used-asset trades do not.

mediumBoss.q: A construction company completes a new warehouse for a retailer. What macroeconomic category applies?
options: Household saving without investment
A transfer of an existing asset
Government consumption spending
New investment in a structure
mediumBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
mediumBoss.feedback: A newly produced warehouse is a structure added to the capital stock, so it is macroeconomic investment.

mediumBoss.q: A household deposits part of its paycheck in a bank. What broad role can that saving play?
options: It automatically becomes the household's GDP investment
It directly creates an equal quantity of physical capital
It can supply funds that the bank channels to borrowers
It removes the funds permanently from the financial system
mediumBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
mediumBoss.feedback: Financial intermediaries can channel saving toward borrowers who finance investment, without making the deposit itself physical investment.

mediumBoss.q: How does greater national saving make more investment possible?
options: It guarantees every proposed project will be profitable
It requires each saver to build a specific machine
It makes more resources available through the financial system
It makes the real interest rate irrelevant
mediumBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
mediumBoss.feedback: Saving frees resources from current consumption and the financial system allocates funds among potential investment projects.

mediumBoss.q: Why is the statement 'each saver finances one identical investment project' incorrect?
options: National saving is unrelated to available financing
Financial markets pool funds and allocate them among borrowers
Only governments can channel funds to firms
Every saver must purchase newly produced equipment
mediumBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
mediumBoss.feedback: The aggregate saving-investment link is mediated through institutions and markets, not one-to-one matching of people and projects.

mediumBoss.q: With T defined as net tax revenue and G as government purchases, which expression gives public saving?
options: Y − T − C
T − G
Y − C − G
G − T + C
mediumBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
mediumBoss.feedback: Under the stated textbook convention, public saving equals net tax revenue minus government purchases.

mediumBoss.q: According to CBO's February 2026 baseline, FY2026 revenues are projected at about $5.6 trillion and outlays at about $7.4 trillion. What fiscal position is projected?
options: A deficit because projected outlays exceed projected revenues
A surplus because projected revenues are positive
A balanced budget because both values are projections
A debt stock of $1.8 trillion
mediumBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
mediumBoss.feedback: CBO projects outlays above revenues, which is a deficit; the published rounded deficit is about $1.9 trillion.

mediumBoss.q: Which statement uses the public-saving convention correctly?
options: T − G, with T net of transfers and G purchases
Total revenues minus all federal outlays is always T − G public saving
T means gross collections and G includes transfers
Public saving is the federal debt stock
mediumBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
mediumBoss.feedback: The notation is valid only when T is net tax revenue, net of transfers, and G is government purchases.

mediumBoss.q: Treasury's Debt to the Penny data list debt held by the public separately from intragovernmental holdings. Why?
options: One is a flow and the other is GDP
Intragovernmental holdings represent Treasury debt owned by foreign investors
They are distinct components of total public debt
Debt held by the public is classified as a current federal outlay
mediumBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
mediumBoss.feedback: The data dictionary separates outside-government holdings from claims held by government accounts.

mediumBoss.q: CBO's February 2026 baseline projects net interest outlays above $1.0 trillion in FY2026, up from $970 billion in FY2025. What is the valid interpretation?
options: Federal debt itself is projected to equal exactly $1.0 trillion
The figures are realized calendar-year revenues collected by Treasury
The annual federal deficit must equal the projected interest outlay
Projected interest outlays rise; neither figure is the debt stock
mediumBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
mediumBoss.feedback: CBO reports projected fiscal-year interest flows, distinct from the accumulated debt stock.

finalBoss.q: A household buys existing shares from another investor. Later, the corporation issues new bonds and uses the proceeds to build a factory. Which statement correctly distinguishes the transactions?
options: Both securities trades are current GDP investment because money changes hands
Only the existing-share purchase is current GDP investment because it changes ownership
Only the new factory is current GDP investment
Neither the bond issue nor the factory affects saving, financing, or current production
finalBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
finalBoss.feedback: Existing-share trades transfer financial claims. Newly issued bonds can channel saving to the firm, but the newly produced factory is the transaction counted as current macroeconomic investment.

finalBoss.q: A firm produces $12 million of goods this year but sells them next year without producing replacements. How are the two years affected, all else equal?
options: Consumption rises this year and inventory investment is unchanged next year
Inventory investment rises this year and falls next year
Inventory investment falls this year and rises again when the goods are sold
The goods count as financial investment in both years because ownership changes
finalBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
finalBoss.feedback: Unsold current production adds $12 million to inventories this year. Selling those previously produced goods next year reduces inventories, creating negative inventory investment then.

finalBoss.q: An investor buys an existing corporate bond from another household, and the issuer receives none of the sale proceeds. Which inference is justified?
options: The issuer's investment rises automatically by the bond's resale price
National saving falls because every secondary-market trade uses saved funds
The trade creates inventory investment because the bond remains unsold by the issuer
It only reallocates an existing financial claim
finalBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
finalBoss.feedback: A secondary-market bond sale changes who owns the claim. With no new proceeds to the issuer and no new production specified, it creates no direct GDP investment.

finalBoss.q: Income is $1,000, net taxes are $180, consumption is $650, and government purchases are $220. If government purchases then rise by $30 with the other values fixed, which result follows?
options: Private saving stays $170; public and national saving fall $30
Private saving falls to $140; public saving is unchanged, shifting investment demand left
Private saving stays $170; public and national saving each rise by $30, shifting supply right
Private saving rises to $200; national saving is unchanged because taxes did not change
finalBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
finalBoss.feedback: Private saving is Y − T − C = $170. Higher G does not change that amount, but it lowers T − G and national saving by $30, so loanable-funds supply shifts left.

finalBoss.q: Private saving rises by $25 billion while public saving falls by $40 billion. What happens in the loanable-funds market, all else equal?
options: National saving rises by $65 billion, shifting supply right and lowering the real rate
National saving rises by $15 billion, shifting investment demand right and raising the real rate
National saving is unchanged because private and public saving always offset one another
National saving falls by $15 billion, shifting supply left and raising the equilibrium real rate
finalBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
finalBoss.feedback: The two components change national saving by +25 − 40 = −$15 billion. Lower national saving shifts loanable-funds supply left, raising the real rate and reducing equilibrium investment.

finalBoss.q: If net taxes rise by $20 while income, consumption, and government purchases stay fixed, what happens to national saving?
options: It rises by $20
It remains unchanged
It falls by $20
It becomes equal to net taxes
finalBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
finalBoss.feedback: Private saving falls by $20 while public saving rises by $20, so their sum and Y − C − G are unchanged.

finalBoss.q: The government collects payroll taxes, sends pension benefits, and buys medical equipment. Which classification is correct?
options: Taxes, benefits, and equipment purchases are all federal revenue
Benefits and equipment both enter government purchases in GDP when paid
Taxes are revenue; both payments are outlays; only equipment is G
Payroll taxes are borrowing
finalBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
finalBoss.feedback: Budget and GDP classifications overlap but are not identical: transfers are outlays without entering G when paid.

finalBoss.q: The annual deficit narrows from $1.5 trillion to $0.7 trillion. Assuming each deficit is financed by borrowing, which statement is correct?
options: Debt rises by less in the second year
Debt falls by $0.8 trillion during the second fiscal year
The second year has a surplus
Debt remains unchanged
finalBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
finalBoss.feedback: Both years have positive deficits, so debt rises under the assumption; only the size of the addition falls.

finalBoss.q: Over four years, the government runs progressively smaller but still positive deficits. Under simplified borrowing finance, what happens?
options: Debt falls each year because every annual deficit is smaller
Debt rises by smaller amounts each year
Debt becomes zero when the fourth and smallest deficit occurs
Public saving becomes positive
finalBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
finalBoss.feedback: A smaller deficit is still a deficit; it adds less to debt but does not reverse the stock by itself.

finalBoss.q: Country A's debt grows 4 percent and nominal GDP grows 7 percent. Country B's debt grows 6 percent and nominal GDP grows 3 percent. Which comparison is correct?
options: A's ratio falls while B's rises
Both debt ratios rise because both nominal debt stocks increase
Both debt ratios fall because nominal GDP increases in both countries
A's debt ratio rises while B's debt ratio falls
finalBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
finalBoss.feedback: A's denominator grows faster than its numerator; B's numerator grows faster than its denominator.

legendaryBoss.q: A software firm develops a new platform for long-term use, buys an existing patent from another firm, and issues shares to finance both activities. Which evaluation is most accurate?
options: All three activities are current intellectual-property investment because each has a price
Only the new platform may be current intellectual-property investment
Only the share issue is current GDP investment because it raises financial capital
The existing patent purchase creates new output, while developing the platform is current consumption
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Qualifying development creates a new productive intangible asset. Buying an existing patent and issuing shares transfer ownership or financial claims rather than independently creating current output.

legendaryBoss.q: Initially Y = $900, T = $150, C = $600, and G = $180. Net taxes then rise by $20 and government purchases rise by $35 while Y and C stay fixed. What changes?
options: Private saving rises $20, public saving rises $15, and national saving rises $35
Private saving falls $20, public saving rises $20, and national saving is unchanged
Private saving is unchanged, public saving falls $35, and national saving falls $15
Private saving falls $20, public saving falls $15, and national saving falls $35
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Higher net taxes reduce private saving by $20. Public saving changes by +$20 − $35 = −$15. Together, national saving falls $35, matching the change in Y − C − G.

legendaryBoss.q: In a closed economy, output is $1,240 billion, consumption is $790 billion and government purchases are $230 billion. Firms planned $250 billion of investment, including planned inventory accumulation. Output and final purchases are realized as stated. Which reconciliation is consistent with national accounting?
options: $220 billion of saving and $250 billion of realized investment, leaving a $30 billion accounting gap
$220 billion of realized saving and investment, including a $30 billion unplanned inventory reduction
$250 billion of realized saving and investment, with consumption automatically $30 billion lower
$220 billion of realized investment, including a $30 billion unplanned inventory increase
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Realized saving is Y − C − G = 1,240 − 790 − 230 = $220 billion. Realized investment includes inventories, so it is also $220 billion. Relative to planned investment of $250 billion, unplanned inventory investment is −$30 billion. Equality of realized aggregates does not require equality of plans at every interest rate.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the graph above. Treat the lines as straight. Starting at A, a technology change shifts D0 horizontally right while S0 stays fixed. The new equilibrium real rate is 10 percent, although the new demand curve is not drawn. What can be inferred about the shift and the quantity response?
options: Demand shifted right by 40 units; equilibrium investment rose by 40 through a rightward shift of S0
Demand shifted right by 80 units; equilibrium investment rose by 80 because saving must match the shift
Demand shifted right by 40 units; equilibrium investment rose by 80 through movement along D0
Demand shifted right by 80 units; equilibrium investment rose by 40 through movement along S0
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
legendaryBoss.feedback: On S0, a 10 percent rate corresponds to 180 units. Old D0 demands 100 units at that rate, so the new demand schedule must be 80 units to the right. Equilibrium investment rises from 140 to 180, or 40 units. The unchanged saving schedule accommodates that quantity through a rate-induced movement; an accounting identity does not force a saving-supply shift.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Loanable-funds graph with S0, D0 and labeled intersection A.
legendaryBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is labeled Quantity of loanable funds; the vertical axis is labeled Real interest rate. Coordinates below are (quantity, rate). The quantity axis has no currency scale. All curves are straight. The solid red line labeled S0 (saving) slopes upward through (0, 1) and (140, 8). The solid blue line labeled D0 (investment) slopes downward through (0, 15) and (140, 8). Point A marks the S0–D0 intersection at (140, 8). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides connect the labeled intersection points to the axes.

legendaryBoss.q: At a real interest rate below equilibrium, desired investment exceeds desired saving. A student claims this disproves S = I in a closed economy. Which response correctly separates the accounting statement from the market adjustment?
options: Realized saving exceeds realized investment until the rate rises; inventory changes are excluded from investment
Realized investment equals desired investment at every rate; the saving identity applies only after the rate adjusts
Realized saving includes the financing gap as foreign saving; the rate rises until that gap disappears
Realized investment, including unplanned inventories, equals realized saving; excess demand for funds puts upward pressure on the rate
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
legendaryBoss.feedback: S = I is an ex-post closed-economy accounting identity, including inventory investment. Planned quantities can disagree at a posted rate; that behavioral imbalance creates upward pressure on the real rate. Market clearing explains compatible plans, not the validity of the identity.

legendaryBoss.q: Initially, desired investment is I = 300 − 10r, with I in billions of dollars and r measured in percentage points. Technology changes only the intercept. The real rate rises from 4 to 7 percent, and equilibrium investment rises by $20 billion. What happened to investment demand, and what would investment have been at the original rate after the technology change?
options: Demand shifted right by $20 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $280 billion
Demand shifted right by $50 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $310 billion
Demand shifted right by $30 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $290 billion
Demand shifted right by $50 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $280 billion
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Initial investment is 300 − 10(4) = $260 billion, so the new equilibrium quantity is $280 billion. The 3-point rate increase reduces quantity demanded by $30 billion along the new schedule. Technology therefore raises demand by $50 billion at every rate, making investment $310 billion at 4 percent.

legendaryBoss.q: A simplified government has only three outlay categories: purchases of current domestic goods and services, transfers, and interest. Purchases rise from $400 billion to $430 billion, transfers from $300 billion to $350 billion, and interest from $50 billion to $70 billion. Revenues rise by $60 billion. Which comparison is correct?
options: The deficit widens by $40 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $100 billion
The deficit narrows by $30 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $40 billion
The deficit widens by $100 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $30 billion
The deficit widens by $40 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $30 billion
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Outlays rise by 30 + 50 + 20 = $100 billion. With revenues up $60 billion, the deficit widens $40 billion. Only the $30 billion increase in current purchases directly increases G; transfers and interest are budget outlays without being current government purchases. No induced output response is being calculated.

legendaryBoss.q: CBO's February 2026 baseline projects a $1.9 trillion FY2026 deficit and debt held by the public equal to 101 percent of GDP at year-end. What distinction is essential?
options: Two realized annual flows
A fiscal-year flow versus a year-end stock ratio
A tax-financed share of outlays versus a projected revenue total
The deficit is accumulated debt
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The CBO figures describe different economic objects and are explicitly projections.

legendaryBoss.q: A deficit reduces public saving at every real rate. A separate household incentive exactly offsets that reduction in planned private saving at every rate, while an investment tax credit also raises desired investment. In the closed-economy loanable-funds model, what can be concluded relative to the initial equilibrium?
options: The saving curve shifts left; the real rate rises and private investment must fall
Both curves are unchanged; exact private-saving offset also cancels the investment tax credit
The saving curve is unchanged; the real rate and equilibrium private investment rise
The saving curve shifts right; private investment rises but the real rate must fall
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The public- and private-saving shifts cancel at every rate, leaving national-saving supply unchanged. The tax credit separately shifts investment demand right. With an upward-sloping saving curve, the new equilibrium has a higher real rate and more private investment. A higher rate alone does not prove crowding out when investment demand also changes.

legendaryBoss.q: CBO’s February 2026 baseline projects debt held by the public at 101 percent of GDP in 2026 and 120 percent in 2036. An analyst claims that nominal debt would therefore rise 19 percent. For that nominal-debt growth claim to be consistent with these displayed ratios, what would nominal GDP have to do?
options: Rise by 19 percent; debt and GDP must grow at the same rate when the ratio increases
Rise by about 0.16 percent; the 19-percentage-point ratio increase is not itself nominal-debt growth
Remain exactly unchanged; subtracting the two ratios gives the percent growth in debt
Fall by about 15.8 percent; a higher debt ratio necessarily implies a smaller economy
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Let GDP growth have factor g. The nominal-debt factor would be (120 / 101)g. Setting it to 1.19 gives g = 1.19(101 / 120) ≈ 1.001583, a 0.16 percent increase. This is a conditional consistency calculation using displayed rounded ratios, not CBO’s GDP projection.

repairQuestions.q: Which activity is macroeconomic investment rather than a financial-asset trade?
options: An investor buys an existing stock
A saver buys an existing bond
A collector resells an old sculpture
A manufacturer installs new production equipment
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
repairQuestions.feedback: New production equipment adds to the capital stock; the other choices transfer ownership of existing assets.

repairQuestions.q: Net tax revenue is $500 and government purchases are $450. What is public saving?
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
repairQuestions.feedback: Using the defined quantities, T − G equals $500 − $450 = +$50.

repairQuestions.q: In the closed-economy model, what aggregate relationship connects national saving and investment?
options: National saving equals investment
Private saving equals consumption
Public saving equals income
Investment equals government purchases
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
repairQuestions.feedback: Both national saving and investment equal Y − C − G in the specified closed-economy model.

repairQuestions.q: A student labels desired investment as the supply of loanable funds. What correction is needed?
options: Investment is supply; consumption is demand
Both investment and saving are demand
Both investment and saving are supply
Investment is demand; national saving is supply
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
repairQuestions.feedback: Borrowers demand funds to finance desired investment, while national saving provides the funds supplied.

repairQuestions.q: If only the real interest rate rises, does the saving curve shift?
options: No, quantity saved rises along the curve
Yes, saving supply shifts right
Yes, saving supply shifts left
No, quantity saved must fall
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
repairQuestions.feedback: A change in the market price causes movement along the saving curve, not a shift.

repairQuestions.q: If national saving increases, which curve shifts?
options: Investment demand shifts right
Investment demand shifts left
Saving supply shifts left
The supply of loanable funds shifts right
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Changes in Saving.
repairQuestions.feedback: National saving is the supply of loanable funds, so an increase shifts that curve right.

repairQuestions.q: Federal revenues are $5 trillion and outlays are $6 trillion. Is the budget in surplus or deficit?
options: Surplus
Deficit
Balanced
Debt-free
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
repairQuestions.feedback: Outlays exceed revenues by $1 trillion, so the federal budget is in deficit.

repairQuestions.q: T is net tax revenue of $700 billion and G is purchases of $600 billion. What is public saving?
options: −$100 billion
+$100 billion
$600 billion
$1.3 trillion
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
repairQuestions.feedback: Subtract government purchases from net tax revenue: $700 billion minus $600 billion equals +$100 billion.

repairQuestions.q: Which transaction is a government purchase rather than a transfer?
options: The federal purchase of new computers
A pension benefit payment
An unemployment benefit payment
An interest payment on debt
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
repairQuestions.feedback: Buying current goods is a government purchase; benefits and interest are outlays but not G purchases.

repairQuestions.q: Which measure describes how much outlays exceed revenues during one year?
options: The debt stock
Debt-to-GDP
The deficit
Intragovernmental holdings
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
repairQuestions.feedback: A deficit is measured over a year; debt is the accumulated amount outstanding at a date.

repairQuestions.q: A government has outlays above revenues. What commonly finances the shortfall?
options: A budget surplus
Lower accumulated debt by definition
Government purchases becoming revenue
Government borrowing
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
repairQuestions.feedback: Borrowing is a common way to finance the annual gap between outlays and revenues.

repairQuestions.q: Which measure equals debt held by the public plus intragovernmental holdings?
options: The annual federal deficit
Annual net interest outlays
Federal government purchases
Total public debt outstanding
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
repairQuestions.feedback: Treasury defines total public debt outstanding as the sum of those two components.

repairQuestions.q: Debt is $15 trillion and GDP is $20 trillion. What is debt-to-GDP?
options: 25 percent
35 percent
75 percent
133 percent
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
repairQuestions.feedback: Divide debt by GDP: 15/20 equals 0.75, or 75 percent.

repairQuestions.q: Under a simplifying assumption, debt is $5 trillion and the annual rate is 2 percent. What is the interest cost?
options: $0.1 trillion
$1.0 trillion
$2.5 trillion
$10 trillion
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
repairQuestions.feedback: Two percent of $5 trillion is $0.1 trillion, or $100 billion.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does household saving connect to later capital formation?
options: Saving is itself always a newly produced capital good
Saved funds must remain idle outside all markets
Financial channels can direct saved funds to investment projects
Capital formation occurs only through household consumption
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The financial system connects the repaired saving idea to firms and households that borrow for new capital investment.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does positive public saving connect the accounting identities to the loanable-funds market?
options: It shifts investment demand by definition
It adds to national saving, the supply of loanable funds
It makes private saving equal zero
It converts government purchases into consumption
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Public saving joins private saving to form national saving, which supplies funds in the closed-economy loanable-funds model.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the accounting identity connect to the loanable-funds model?
options: Consumption becomes the demand for loanable funds
Government purchases become the real interest rate
Every saver chooses the same investment project
National saving supplies funds that finance aggregate investment
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The closed-economy identity provides the aggregate connection; the loanable-funds market explains coordination through the real interest rate.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which side of the loanable-funds market represents saving?
options: The demand side
The price axis
The supply side
The investment schedule
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: National saving supplies the funds available to borrowers in the closed-economy model.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a curve shift lead to a movement on the other side of the market?
options: Both curves must shift by equal distances
The unchanged curve becomes vertical
The quantity axis determines the new price
The shift changes equilibrium price, altering quantity on the unchanged curve
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A non-interest shock shifts one curve; the resulting rate change causes movement along the other curve.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does greater national saving connect to investment?
options: More supply raises financing cost and lowers investment
Saving shifts investment demand left by definition
More supply lowers financing cost and raises equilibrium investment
Saving removes all funds from financial markets
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Changes in Saving.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The supply shift lowers the real interest rate, encouraging more investment projects to be financed.

bridgeQuestions.q: A federal budget records revenues below outlays. What financing issue follows from that accounting result?
options: The shortfall becomes additional tax revenue in the same year
Government purchases become zero
The shortfall must be financed, commonly through borrowing
Existing federal debt disappears
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A deficit is an annual financing gap; borrowing is a common way to cover it.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does negative public saving matter beyond the federal budget?
options: It directly fixes the economy's nominal exchange rate
It makes positive private saving impossible by definition
It reduces one component of national saving
It determines the national money supply without monetary policy
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Negative public saving lowers national saving, all else equal, and therefore reduces the funds available to finance investment in the loanable-funds model.

bridgeQuestions.q: A federal benefit payment is an outlay but not government purchases in GDP when paid. When can it affect measured GDP?
options: When Treasury classifies the benefit as mandatory spending
When recipients buy newly produced goods or services
Immediately, because every federal outlay enters G in GDP
Only after the outstanding federal debt stock begins to fall
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The transfer itself is not production; later consumption of current final output can enter GDP.

bridgeQuestions.q: A government runs a deficit and finances it entirely by borrowing. What happens next in the simplified example?
options: The debt stock is erased
The budget becomes balanced automatically
The deficit becomes revenue
The debt stock increases
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Borrowing to cover the annual shortfall adds to accumulated debt under the stated simplification.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which framework traces how lower public saving can affect interest rates and private investment?
options: Saving, investment, and loanable funds
The consumer price index and inflation measurement alone
Monopoly pricing
The production-possibilities frontier without financial markets
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The loanable-funds model traces how lower national saving can raise the real interest rate and reduce private investment.

bridgeQuestions.q: Treasury defines debt held by the public as a distinct debt measure. What additional quantity is needed to express that measure relative to the economy?
options: GDP for a matching period
The annual inflation rate alone
Government purchases only
The number of Treasury securities
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A debt-to-GDP ratio divides a specified debt stock by a compatible GDP measure.

bridgeQuestions.q: CBO projects debt held by the public at 101 percent of GDP in 2026. What must remain explicit when using that ratio?
options: Only the general word debt without a measure label
The value of intragovernmental holdings without a GDP denominator
A statement that the projected ratio has already been realized
The debt measure and projected year
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The ratio identifies debt held by the public, the year, and its projected status.

bridgeQuestions.q: If net interest outlays rise while revenues and all other outlays are unchanged, what happens to the budget balance?
options: It improves automatically
It shifts toward deficit
It becomes a debt-to-GDP ratio instead of a budget balance
It remains unchanged because interest is excluded from federal outlays
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher interest outlays reduce revenues minus total outlays when everything else is fixed.

distinguish_saving_and_investment.q: Which activity is macroeconomic investment rather than a financial-asset trade?
options: An investor buys an existing stock
A saver buys an existing bond
A collector resells an old sculpture
A manufacturer installs new production equipment
distinguish_saving_and_investment.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
distinguish_saving_and_investment.feedback: New production equipment adds to the capital stock; the other choices transfer ownership of existing assets.

calculate_national_saving.q: Net tax revenue is $500 and government purchases are $450. What is public saving?
calculate_national_saving.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
calculate_national_saving.feedback: Using the defined quantities, T − G equals $500 − $450 = +$50.

apply_closed_economy_saving_identity.q: In the closed-economy model, what aggregate relationship connects national saving and investment?
options: National saving equals investment
Private saving equals consumption
Public saving equals income
Investment equals government purchases
apply_closed_economy_saving_identity.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
apply_closed_economy_saving_identity.feedback: Both national saving and investment equal Y − C − G in the specified closed-economy model.

analyze_loanable_funds_equilibrium.q: A student labels desired investment as the supply of loanable funds. What correction is needed?
options: Investment is supply; consumption is demand
Both investment and saving are demand
Both investment and saving are supply
Investment is demand; national saving is supply
analyze_loanable_funds_equilibrium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
analyze_loanable_funds_equilibrium.feedback: Borrowers demand funds to finance desired investment, while national saving provides the funds supplied.

distinguish_movement_from_shift_loanable.q: If only the real interest rate rises, does the saving curve shift?
options: No, quantity saved rises along the curve
Yes, saving supply shifts right
Yes, saving supply shifts left
No, quantity saved must fall
distinguish_movement_from_shift_loanable.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
distinguish_movement_from_shift_loanable.feedback: A change in the market price causes movement along the saving curve, not a shift.

analyze_saving_supply_shift.q: If national saving increases, which curve shifts?
options: Investment demand shifts right
Investment demand shifts left
Saving supply shifts left
The supply of loanable funds shifts right
analyze_saving_supply_shift.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Changes in Saving.
analyze_saving_supply_shift.feedback: National saving is the supply of loanable funds, so an increase shifts that curve right.

identify_budget_position.q: Federal revenues are $5 trillion and outlays are $6 trillion. Is the budget in surplus or deficit?
options: Surplus
Deficit
Balanced
Debt-free
identify_budget_position.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
identify_budget_position.feedback: Outlays exceed revenues by $1 trillion, so the federal budget is in deficit.

calculate_public_saving.q: T is net tax revenue of $700 billion and G is purchases of $600 billion. What is public saving?
options: −$100 billion
+$100 billion
$600 billion
$1.3 trillion
calculate_public_saving.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
calculate_public_saving.feedback: Subtract government purchases from net tax revenue: $700 billion minus $600 billion equals +$100 billion.

distinguish_purchase_transfer.q: Which transaction is a government purchase rather than a transfer?
options: The federal purchase of new computers
A pension benefit payment
An unemployment benefit payment
An interest payment on debt
distinguish_purchase_transfer.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
distinguish_purchase_transfer.feedback: Buying current goods is a government purchase; benefits and interest are outlays but not G purchases.

distinguish_deficit_and_debt.q: Which measure describes how much outlays exceed revenues during one year?
options: The debt stock
Debt-to-GDP
The deficit
Intragovernmental holdings
distinguish_deficit_and_debt.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
distinguish_deficit_and_debt.feedback: A deficit is measured over a year; debt is the accumulated amount outstanding at a date.

connect_deficit_borrowing.q: A government has outlays above revenues. What commonly finances the shortfall?
options: A budget surplus
Lower accumulated debt by definition
Government purchases becoming revenue
Government borrowing
connect_deficit_borrowing.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
connect_deficit_borrowing.feedback: Borrowing is a common way to finance the annual gap between outlays and revenues.

distinguish_debt_measures.q: Which measure equals debt held by the public plus intragovernmental holdings?
options: The annual federal deficit
Annual net interest outlays
Federal government purchases
Total public debt outstanding
distinguish_debt_measures.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
distinguish_debt_measures.feedback: Treasury defines total public debt outstanding as the sum of those two components.

calculate_debt_to_gdp.q: Debt is $15 trillion and GDP is $20 trillion. What is debt-to-GDP?
options: 25 percent
35 percent
75 percent
133 percent
calculate_debt_to_gdp.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
calculate_debt_to_gdp.feedback: Divide debt by GDP: 15/20 equals 0.75, or 75 percent.

calculate_simple_interest_cost.q: Under a simplifying assumption, debt is $5 trillion and the annual rate is 2 percent. What is the interest cost?
options: $0.1 trillion
$1.0 trillion
$2.5 trillion
$10 trillion
calculate_simple_interest_cost.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
calculate_simple_interest_cost.feedback: Two percent of $5 trillion is $0.1 trillion, or $100 billion.

distinguish_saving_and_investment.q: How does household saving connect to later capital formation?
options: Saving is itself always a newly produced capital good
Saved funds must remain idle outside all markets
Financial channels can direct saved funds to investment projects
Capital formation occurs only through household consumption
distinguish_saving_and_investment.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
distinguish_saving_and_investment.feedback: The financial system connects the repaired saving idea to firms and households that borrow for new capital investment.

calculate_national_saving.q: How does positive public saving connect the accounting identities to the loanable-funds market?
options: It shifts investment demand by definition
It adds to national saving, the supply of loanable funds
It makes private saving equal zero
It converts government purchases into consumption
calculate_national_saving.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
calculate_national_saving.feedback: Public saving joins private saving to form national saving, which supplies funds in the closed-economy loanable-funds model.

apply_closed_economy_saving_identity.q: How does the accounting identity connect to the loanable-funds model?
options: Consumption becomes the demand for loanable funds
Government purchases become the real interest rate
Every saver chooses the same investment project
National saving supplies funds that finance aggregate investment
apply_closed_economy_saving_identity.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
apply_closed_economy_saving_identity.feedback: The closed-economy identity provides the aggregate connection; the loanable-funds market explains coordination through the real interest rate.

analyze_loanable_funds_equilibrium.q: Which side of the loanable-funds market represents saving?
options: The demand side
The price axis
The supply side
The investment schedule
analyze_loanable_funds_equilibrium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
analyze_loanable_funds_equilibrium.feedback: National saving supplies the funds available to borrowers in the closed-economy model.

distinguish_movement_from_shift_loanable.q: How does a curve shift lead to a movement on the other side of the market?
options: Both curves must shift by equal distances
The unchanged curve becomes vertical
The quantity axis determines the new price
The shift changes equilibrium price, altering quantity on the unchanged curve
distinguish_movement_from_shift_loanable.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
distinguish_movement_from_shift_loanable.feedback: A non-interest shock shifts one curve; the resulting rate change causes movement along the other curve.

analyze_saving_supply_shift.q: How does greater national saving connect to investment?
options: More supply raises financing cost and lowers investment
Saving shifts investment demand left by definition
More supply lowers financing cost and raises equilibrium investment
Saving removes all funds from financial markets
analyze_saving_supply_shift.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Changes in Saving.
analyze_saving_supply_shift.feedback: The supply shift lowers the real interest rate, encouraging more investment projects to be financed.

connect_balance_to_borrowing.q: A federal budget records revenues below outlays. What financing issue follows from that accounting result?
options: The shortfall becomes additional tax revenue in the same year
Government purchases become zero
The shortfall must be financed, commonly through borrowing
Existing federal debt disappears
connect_balance_to_borrowing.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
connect_balance_to_borrowing.feedback: A deficit is an annual financing gap; borrowing is a common way to cover it.

connect_public_to_national_saving.q: Why does negative public saving matter beyond the federal budget?
options: It directly fixes the economy's nominal exchange rate
It makes positive private saving impossible by definition
It reduces one component of national saving
It determines the national money supply without monetary policy
connect_public_to_national_saving.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
connect_public_to_national_saving.feedback: Negative public saving lowers national saving, all else equal, and therefore reduces the funds available to finance investment in the loanable-funds model.

connect_outlay_to_gdp.q: A federal benefit payment is an outlay but not government purchases in GDP when paid. When can it affect measured GDP?
options: When Treasury classifies the benefit as mandatory spending
When recipients buy newly produced goods or services
Immediately, because every federal outlay enters G in GDP
Only after the outstanding federal debt stock begins to fall
connect_outlay_to_gdp.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
connect_outlay_to_gdp.feedback: The transfer itself is not production; later consumption of current final output can enter GDP.

connect_deficit_to_debt.q: A government runs a deficit and finances it entirely by borrowing. What happens next in the simplified example?
options: The debt stock is erased
The budget becomes balanced automatically
The deficit becomes revenue
The debt stock increases
connect_deficit_to_debt.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
connect_deficit_to_debt.feedback: Borrowing to cover the annual shortfall adds to accumulated debt under the stated simplification.

connect_borrowing_to_phase_two.q: Which framework traces how lower public saving can affect interest rates and private investment?
options: Saving, investment, and loanable funds
The consumer price index and inflation measurement alone
Monopoly pricing
The production-possibilities frontier without financial markets
connect_borrowing_to_phase_two.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
connect_borrowing_to_phase_two.feedback: The loanable-funds model traces how lower national saving can raise the real interest rate and reduce private investment.

connect_debt_measure_to_ratio.q: Treasury defines debt held by the public as a distinct debt measure. What additional quantity is needed to express that measure relative to the economy?
options: GDP for a matching period
The annual inflation rate alone
Government purchases only
The number of Treasury securities
connect_debt_measure_to_ratio.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Measures of Federal Debt.
connect_debt_measure_to_ratio.feedback: A debt-to-GDP ratio divides a specified debt stock by a compatible GDP measure.

connect_cbo_ratio_to_measure.q: CBO projects debt held by the public at 101 percent of GDP in 2026. What must remain explicit when using that ratio?
options: Only the general word debt without a measure label
The value of intragovernmental holdings without a GDP denominator
A statement that the projected ratio has already been realized
The debt measure and projected year
connect_cbo_ratio_to_measure.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Debt-to-GDP.
connect_cbo_ratio_to_measure.feedback: The ratio identifies debt held by the public, the year, and its projected status.

connect_interest_to_budget_balance.q: If net interest outlays rise while revenues and all other outlays are unchanged, what happens to the budget balance?
options: It improves automatically
It shifts toward deficit
It becomes a debt-to-GDP ratio instead of a budget balance
It remains unchanged because interest is excluded from federal outlays
connect_interest_to_budget_balance.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Interest Costs and Debt Service.
connect_interest_to_budget_balance.feedback: Higher interest outlays reduce revenues minus total outlays when everything else is fixed.
