saving-and-investment-identities.title: Saving, Investment, and National-Saving Identities
saving-and-investment-identities.description: Apply private, public, and national saving identities and the saving-investment relationship.

objectiveLabels.SLF3: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

easy.q: If government purchases rise by $30 with income and consumption fixed, what happens to national saving?
options: It rises by $30
It remains unchanged
It falls by $30
It falls by net taxes
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
easy.feedback: From S = Y − C − G, a $30 increase in G lowers national saving by $30, other terms fixed.

easy.q: Why must a saving question define T before using Y − T − C or T − G?
options: T must always mean total federal debt
T must include every government outlay
T must consistently mean net taxes in both expressions
T must equal household consumption
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
easy.feedback: The private- and public-saving formulas share T, so a consistent net-tax definition prevents mixing textbook saving with total-budget accounting.

easy.q: How does the closed-economy identity imply I = Y − C − G?
options: Subtract consumption and government purchases from both sides
Add net exports to both sides
Set private saving equal to taxes
Replace investment with consumption
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
easy.feedback: Rearranging Y = C + I + G yields I = Y − C − G.

easy.q: In a closed economy, a student says each household's saving must equal one firm's investment. What is the correction?
options: S = I is an aggregate identity mediated by the financial system
Each saver must buy one physical machine
Only public saving can finance investment
The equality applies only to individual bank accounts
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
easy.feedback: The equality concerns economy-wide totals; intermediaries and markets pool saving and allocate financing across borrowers.

easy.q: Output is $2,000, consumption is $1,250, and government purchases are $450 in a closed economy. What is investment?
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
easy.feedback: Rearranging the closed-economy expenditure identity gives I = $2,000 − $1,250 − $450 = $300.

medium.q: Net tax revenue is $240 and government purchases are $290. What is public saving?
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
medium.feedback: Public saving is T − G, so $240 − $290 = −$50 under the stated net-tax convention.

medium.q: Using the same economy with private saving of $150 and public saving of −$30, what is national saving?
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
medium.feedback: Adding the two components gives national saving of $150 − $30 = $120.

medium.q: Consumption falls by $25 while income and government purchases remain fixed. What happens to national saving?
options: It falls by $25
It remains unchanged
It rises by net taxes
It rises by $25
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
medium.feedback: Because S = Y − C − G, lower consumption leaves $25 more national saving.

medium.q: A table lists total federal revenues and total outlays including transfers and interest. What does revenues minus outlays measure directly?
options: Public saving T − G under every definition
The federal budget balance
Private saving Y − T − C
National saving Y − C − G
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
medium.feedback: Total revenues minus total outlays is the budget balance; it should not be relabeled T − G unless the specified components match net taxes and purchases.

medium.q: Private saving falls by $15 while public saving rises by $35. What happens to national saving?
options: It rises by $20
It falls by $20
It rises by $50
It remains unchanged
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
medium.feedback: National saving changes by the sum of component changes: −$15 + $35 = +$20.

medium.q: In a closed economy, Y is $1,500, C is $900, and G is $350. What are saving and investment?
options: Both are $350
Saving is $600 and investment is $250
Both are $250
Saving is $250 and investment is $900
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
medium.feedback: Y − C − G equals $250; in the closed-economy model both national saving and investment equal that amount.

medium.q: Consumption rises by $40 in a closed economy while output and government purchases are fixed. What happens to saving and investment?
options: Both rise by $40
Both fall by $40
Saving falls but investment rises
Neither aggregate changes
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
medium.feedback: The increase in C reduces Y − C − G by $40, lowering both national saving and investment in the closed-economy identity.

medium.q: Which claim improperly extends the closed-economy identity?
options: National saving equals Y − C − G in the stated closed model
The financial system connects savers and borrowers
Aggregate saving can finance investment through markets
Domestic saving must equal domestic investment in every open economy
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
medium.feedback: Open economies can finance domestic investment with international flows, so the domestic S = I statement requires the closed-economy qualifier.

medium.q: What role does the financial system play when closed-economy saving equals investment?
options: It requires identical saving from every household
It eliminates all differences in project profitability
It reallocates aggregate saving among borrowers and projects
It turns every security trade into new capital
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
medium.feedback: Intermediation explains how economy-wide saving can finance investment without one-to-one matching between individual savers and firms.

hard.q: Output rises by $100, consumption rises by $70, and government purchases rise by $10. What happens to national saving and loanable-funds supply?
options: National saving rises by $20, so loanable-funds supply shifts right
National saving falls by $20, so loanable-funds supply shifts left
National saving rises by $180, so investment demand shifts right
National saving is unchanged because output and spending all increased
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
hard.feedback: Using S = Y − C − G, the change is +100 − 70 − 10 = +$20. Higher national saving shifts the loanable-funds supply curve right.

hard.q: Net taxes are $320 and government purchases are $280. Private saving then falls by $20 while fiscal quantities remain fixed. What follows?
options: Public saving falls to $20, but national saving remains unchanged
Public saving remains $40, while national saving rises $20 and supply shifts right
Public saving rises to $60, shifting investment demand rather than loanable-funds supply
Public saving stays $40; national saving falls $20
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
hard.feedback: Public saving remains T − G = $40 because fiscal quantities do not change. The $20 decline in private saving therefore lowers national saving and shifts supply left.

hard.q: National saving is initially $420 billion in a closed economy. Improved technology then raises desired investment at every real interest rate. What is the adjustment?
options: Investment stays permanently at $420 billion because the identity prevents demand from shifting
Loanable-funds supply shifts right by exactly the technology improvement, leaving the rate fixed
The identity is violated because desired investment can never differ from saving, even away from equilibrium
Investment demand shifts right, creating upward rate pressure until planned saving and investment are equal again
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
hard.feedback: The accounting identity does not freeze behavior. Higher expected returns shift investment demand right; the real rate adjusts, inducing movements along both curves toward a new equilibrium equality.

hard.q: Government purchases fall by $25 billion in a closed economy with output fixed and the consumption schedule unchanged at each given real rate, while firms also become more optimistic about future sales. Which market description is complete?
options: Only supply shifts right, so both quantity and the real rate must rise
Only investment demand shifts right, so quantity rises and the real rate falls
Both curves shift right; quantity rises and the rate is ambiguous
Both curves shift left, so quantity falls while the real-rate effect is ambiguous
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
hard.feedback: At each given real rate, lower purchases raise planned national saving by $25 billion and shift supply right. Stronger sales expectations shift investment demand right. Both raise equilibrium quantity, but their opposing rate pressures make the rate depend on relative shift magnitudes.

hard.q: Private saving is $360 billion and public saving is −$60 billion. If desired investment at the current real rate is $340 billion, what pressure should move the closed-economy market toward equilibrium?
options: Excess saving puts downward pressure on the real rate, increasing the gap
Excess demand raises the real rate toward equilibrium
Investment demand shifts left automatically by $40 billion because S = I is an identity
Loanable-funds supply shifts right automatically until both quantities equal $360 billion
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
hard.feedback: National saving is $300 billion, below desired investment of $340 billion at the current rate. Excess demand pushes the rate upward, causing movements along the curves toward equilibrium.

elite.q: Households reduce current consumption and buy a firm's newly issued bonds. The firm uses the proceeds for new machinery and to purchase an existing office building. Which chain is economically correct?
options: Both firm purchases are current GDP investment because both use borrowed funds
The bond purchase is physical investment, while neither firm purchase enters GDP
Household saving enters GDP directly, and the machinery is only a financial asset
Saving finances the firm, but only the new machinery is current GDP investment
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
elite.feedback: The bond market channels household saving to the borrower. New machinery is current production and GDP investment; transferring an existing building is not new production.

elite.q: At every given real interest rate, planned private saving increases by $25 billion, but a larger deficit reduces public saving by $40 billion. With investment demand unchanged, which sequence follows?
options: National saving rises by $65 billion; supply shifts right, the real rate falls, and investment rises
National saving falls by $15 billion; supply shifts left, the real rate rises, and investment falls
National saving falls by $15 billion; investment demand shifts left, lowering both rate and quantity
National saving rises by $15 billion; supply shifts right, but investment necessarily falls
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
elite.feedback: The public-saving decline is larger than the private-saving increase, so national saving falls by $15 billion. Supply shifts left, raising financing costs and crowding out investment along demand.

elite.q: In a closed economy, at every given real interest rate, planned private saving rises by $20 billion while public saving falls by $35 billion. At the same time, new technology raises desired investment. What can be concluded without knowing the investment-demand shift magnitude?
options: Both curves shift right; quantity rises, while the real rate is ambiguous
Supply shifts left only; both the real rate and quantity must fall
Investment demand shifts right only; the real rate rises and quantity must rise
Supply shifts left, demand shifts right; the rate rises and quantity is ambiguous
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
elite.feedback: At each given real rate, planned national saving falls by $15 billion, shifting supply left. Technology shifts investment demand right. Both shifts raise the real rate, but their quantity effects oppose one another; the final change in realized saving and investment is therefore not fixed at −$15 billion.

boss.q: Which action is saving in the macroeconomic sense?
options: Setting aside current income for future use
Buying newly produced factory equipment
Building a newly constructed apartment
Adding unsold goods to business inventories
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
boss.feedback: Saving is current income not used for consumption; the other choices are forms of new macroeconomic investment.

boss.q: Which purchase is counted as new macroeconomic investment in GDP?
options: A household buys an existing corporate share
A firm buys newly produced machinery
An investor buys an existing government bond
A collector buys a previously owned painting
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
boss.feedback: New production equipment expands the capital stock and is GDP investment; secondary financial and used-asset trades do not.

boss.q: A household buys existing shares from another investor. Later, the corporation issues new bonds and uses the proceeds to build a factory. Which statement correctly distinguishes the transactions?
options: Both securities trades are current GDP investment because money changes hands
Only the existing-share purchase is current GDP investment because it changes ownership
Only the new factory is current GDP investment
Neither the bond issue nor the factory affects saving, financing, or current production
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
boss.feedback: Existing-share trades transfer financial claims. Newly issued bonds can channel saving to the firm, but the newly produced factory is the transaction counted as current macroeconomic investment.

boss.q: A construction company completes a new warehouse for a retailer. What macroeconomic category applies?
options: Household saving without investment
A transfer of an existing asset
Government consumption spending
New investment in a structure
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
boss.feedback: A newly produced warehouse is a structure added to the capital stock, so it is macroeconomic investment.

boss.q: Why does construction of a new home count as investment in GDP?
options: It creates a new long-lived residential asset
Every household purchase is classified as investment
The buyer must have purchased an existing stock
Residential services are excluded from production
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
boss.feedback: GDP conventions treat new residential construction as investment because it adds a durable structure that yields housing services.

boss.q: A firm produces $12 million of goods this year but sells them next year without producing replacements. How are the two years affected, all else equal?
options: Consumption rises this year and inventory investment is unchanged next year
Inventory investment rises this year and falls next year
Inventory investment falls this year and rises again when the goods are sold
The goods count as financial investment in both years because ownership changes
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
boss.feedback: Unsold current production adds $12 million to inventories this year. Selling those previously produced goods next year reduces inventories, creating negative inventory investment then.

boss.q: A household deposits part of its paycheck in a bank. What broad role can that saving play?
options: It automatically becomes the household's GDP investment
It directly creates an equal quantity of physical capital
It can supply funds that the bank channels to borrowers
It removes the funds permanently from the financial system
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
boss.feedback: Financial intermediaries can channel saving toward borrowers who finance investment, without making the deposit itself physical investment.

boss.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes financial investment from macroeconomic investment?
options: Financial assets can change ownership without creating new capital
Every financial-asset trade adds equally to current GDP investment
Macroeconomic investment means purchasing only stocks and bonds
New equipment is saving rather than macroeconomic investment
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
boss.feedback: Trading an existing claim need not add to current production, while new equipment, structures, inventories, and qualifying intellectual property do.

boss.q: How does greater national saving make more investment possible?
options: It guarantees every proposed project will be profitable
It requires each saver to build a specific machine
It makes more resources available through the financial system
It makes the real interest rate irrelevant
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
boss.feedback: Saving frees resources from current consumption and the financial system allocates funds among potential investment projects.

boss.q: An investor buys an existing corporate bond from another household, and the issuer receives none of the sale proceeds. Which inference is justified?
options: The issuer's investment rises automatically by the bond's resale price
National saving falls because every secondary-market trade uses saved funds
The trade creates inventory investment because the bond remains unsold by the issuer
It only reallocates an existing financial claim
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
boss.feedback: A secondary-market bond sale changes who owns the claim. With no new proceeds to the issuer and no new production specified, it creates no direct GDP investment.

boss.q: Which institution is acting as a financial intermediary?
options: A bank accepts deposits and makes business loans
A factory converts steel into new machinery
A retailer sells newly produced consumer goods
A household consumes services from an existing home
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
boss.feedback: A financial intermediary gathers funds from savers and supplies financing to borrowers rather than producing the capital good itself.

boss.q: Why is the statement 'each saver finances one identical investment project' incorrect?
options: National saving is unrelated to available financing
Financial markets pool funds and allocate them among borrowers
Only governments can channel funds to firms
Every saver must purchase newly produced equipment
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
boss.feedback: The aggregate saving-investment link is mediated through institutions and markets, not one-to-one matching of people and projects.

boss.q: Income is $1,000, net taxes are $180, consumption is $650, and government purchases are $220. If government purchases then rise by $30 with the other values fixed, which result follows?
options: Private saving stays $170; public and national saving fall $30
Private saving falls to $140; public saving is unchanged, shifting investment demand left
Private saving stays $170; public and national saving each rise by $30, shifting supply right
Private saving rises to $200; national saving is unchanged because taxes did not change
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
boss.feedback: Private saving is Y − T − C = $170. Higher G does not change that amount, but it lowers T − G and national saving by $30, so loanable-funds supply shifts left.

boss.q: With T defined as net tax revenue and G as government purchases, which expression gives public saving?
options: Y − T − C
T − G
Y − C − G
G − T + C
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
boss.feedback: Under the stated textbook convention, public saving equals net tax revenue minus government purchases.

boss.q: Which expression gives national saving in the stated closed-economy accounting model?
options: Y − T − C
T − G
Y − C − G
C + I + G
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
boss.feedback: Adding private saving Y − T − C and public saving T − G cancels T, leaving Y − C − G.

boss.q: Private saving rises by $25 billion while public saving falls by $40 billion. What happens in the loanable-funds market, all else equal?
options: National saving rises by $65 billion, shifting supply right and lowering the real rate
National saving rises by $15 billion, shifting investment demand right and raising the real rate
National saving is unchanged because private and public saving always offset one another
National saving falls by $15 billion, shifting supply left and raising the equilibrium real rate
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
boss.feedback: The two components change national saving by +25 − 40 = −$15 billion. Lower national saving shifts loanable-funds supply left, raising the real rate and reducing equilibrium investment.

boss.q: Income is $1,200, consumption is $760, and government purchases are $260. What is national saving?
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
boss.feedback: National saving equals Y − C − G, so $1,200 − $760 − $260 = $180.

boss.q: If net taxes rise by $20 while income, consumption, and government purchases stay fixed, what happens to national saving?
options: It rises by $20
It remains unchanged
It falls by $20
It becomes equal to net taxes
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
boss.feedback: Private saving falls by $20 while public saving rises by $20, so their sum and Y − C − G are unchanged.

legendaryBoss.q: A software firm develops a new platform for long-term use, buys an existing patent from another firm, and issues shares to finance both activities. Which evaluation is most accurate?
options: All three activities are current intellectual-property investment because each has a price
Only the new platform may be current intellectual-property investment
Only the share issue is current GDP investment because it raises financial capital
The existing patent purchase creates new output, while developing the platform is current consumption
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Qualifying development creates a new productive intangible asset. Buying an existing patent and issuing shares transfer ownership or financial claims rather than independently creating current output.

legendaryBoss.q: Initially Y = $900, T = $150, C = $600, and G = $180. Net taxes then rise by $20 and government purchases rise by $35 while Y and C stay fixed. What changes?
options: Private saving rises $20, public saving rises $15, and national saving rises $35
Private saving falls $20, public saving rises $20, and national saving is unchanged
Private saving is unchanged, public saving falls $35, and national saving falls $15
Private saving falls $20, public saving falls $15, and national saving falls $35
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Higher net taxes reduce private saving by $20. Public saving changes by +$20 − $35 = −$15. Together, national saving falls $35, matching the change in Y − C − G.

legendaryBoss.q: In a closed economy, output is $1,240 billion, consumption is $790 billion and government purchases are $230 billion. Firms planned $250 billion of investment, including planned inventory accumulation. Output and final purchases are realized as stated. Which reconciliation is consistent with national accounting?
options: $220 billion of saving and $250 billion of realized investment, leaving a $30 billion accounting gap
$220 billion of realized saving and investment, including a $30 billion unplanned inventory reduction
$250 billion of realized saving and investment, with consumption automatically $30 billion lower
$220 billion of realized investment, including a $30 billion unplanned inventory increase
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Realized saving is Y − C − G = 1,240 − 790 − 230 = $220 billion. Realized investment includes inventories, so it is also $220 billion. Relative to planned investment of $250 billion, unplanned inventory investment is −$30 billion. Equality of realized aggregates does not require equality of plans at every interest rate.

repairQuestions.q: Which activity is macroeconomic investment rather than a financial-asset trade?
options: An investor buys an existing stock
A saver buys an existing bond
A collector resells an old sculpture
A manufacturer installs new production equipment
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
repairQuestions.feedback: New production equipment adds to the capital stock; the other choices transfer ownership of existing assets.

repairQuestions.q: Net tax revenue is $500 and government purchases are $450. What is public saving?
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
repairQuestions.feedback: Using the defined quantities, T − G equals $500 − $450 = +$50.

repairQuestions.q: In the closed-economy model, what aggregate relationship connects national saving and investment?
options: National saving equals investment
Private saving equals consumption
Public saving equals income
Investment equals government purchases
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
repairQuestions.feedback: Both national saving and investment equal Y − C − G in the specified closed-economy model.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does household saving connect to later capital formation?
options: Saving is itself always a newly produced capital good
Saved funds must remain idle outside all markets
Financial channels can direct saved funds to investment projects
Capital formation occurs only through household consumption
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The financial system connects the repaired saving idea to firms and households that borrow for new capital investment.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does positive public saving connect the accounting identities to the loanable-funds market?
options: It shifts investment demand by definition
It adds to national saving, the supply of loanable funds
It makes private saving equal zero
It converts government purchases into consumption
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Public saving joins private saving to form national saving, which supplies funds in the closed-economy loanable-funds model.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the accounting identity connect to the loanable-funds model?
options: Consumption becomes the demand for loanable funds
Government purchases become the real interest rate
Every saver chooses the same investment project
National saving supplies funds that finance aggregate investment
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The closed-economy identity provides the aggregate connection; the loanable-funds market explains coordination through the real interest rate.

loanable-funds-equilibrium.title: Loanable-Funds Equilibrium
loanable-funds-equilibrium.description: Analyze loanable-funds equilibrium and distinguish movement along curves from curve shifts.

easy.q: Refer to the graph above. What quantity of loanable funds is exchanged at equilibrium?
options: 70 units
210 units
140 units
280 units
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
easy.feedback: The vertical guide from A reaches 140 on the quantity axis, the equilibrium amount supplied and demanded.

easy.q: Refer to the graph above. At a real interest rate below 8 percent, which imbalance appears?
options: Saving supplied exceeds investment demanded
Saving and investment remain equal
Investment demanded exceeds saving supplied
Both curves shift to the left
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
easy.feedback: Below A, D0 gives a larger quantity than S0, creating excess demand for loanable funds.

options: A is 8 units at a 140 percent rate
A is 210 units at a 10 percent rate
A is 140 units at an 8 percent real rate
A is 70 units at a 6 percent rate
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
easy.feedback: The guides from A identify Q = 140 on the horizontal axis and r = 8 percent on the vertical axis.

easy.q: Why does investment demand slope downward?
options: More projects pass the profitability test at higher rates
Saving automatically falls whenever investment rises
Fewer projects are profitable at higher real borrowing costs
The real interest rate is unrelated to project cost
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
easy.feedback: As the real cost of financing rises, marginal investment projects no longer earn enough to be undertaken.

easy.q: A higher real interest rate by itself causes what change in saving?
options: A movement upward along the saving curve
A rightward shift of the saving curve
A leftward shift of investment demand
A movement downward along investment demand
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
easy.feedback: The real interest rate is on the vertical axis, so its change alters quantity supplied along an unchanged saving curve.

easy.q: Which event causes movement along both loanable-funds curves rather than shifting either one?
options: A change in the real interest rate
A change in household saving preferences
A change in expected business profitability
A change in public saving
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
easy.feedback: Because the real interest rate is the market price on the vertical axis, its change alters quantities along existing curves.

easy.q: After investment demand shifts right, the equilibrium rate rises. How should the saving response be described?
options: A movement up along the saving curve
A rightward shift of saving supply
A leftward shift of saving supply
A movement down along investment demand
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
easy.feedback: The demand shock raises the rate, which increases the quantity saved along the unchanged supply curve.

medium.q: Refer to the graph above. Which labeled curve represents desired investment?
options: D0, the downward-sloping blue curve
S0, the upward-sloping red curve
The horizontal guide through 8 percent
The vertical guide through 140 units
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
medium.feedback: The graph labels the downward-sloping demand for loanable funds as D0 (investment).
medium.imageAlt: Loanable-funds graph with S0, D0 and labeled intersection A.

The quantity axis has no currency scale. All curves are straight. The solid red line labeled S0 (saving) slopes upward through (0, 1) and (140, 8). The solid blue line labeled D0 (investment) slopes downward through (0, 15) and (140, 8). Point A marks the S0–D0 intersection at (140, 8). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides connect the labeled intersection points to the axes.

medium.q: Refer to the graph above. What does point A establish about planned saving and investment?
options: Saving exceeds investment by 140
Investment exceeds saving by 8 percent
Both quantities are zero at equilibrium
Their aggregate quantities are equal at 140
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
medium.feedback: Point A is the S0-D0 intersection, so the two planned quantities are equal at 140 units.

Dashed horizontal and vertical guides connect the labeled intersection points to the axes.

medium.q: Refer to the graph above. Which variable acts as the market price, and where is it measured?
options: The quantity of loanable funds on the horizontal axis
The real interest rate on the vertical axis
National saving along the S0 curve
Desired investment along the D0 curve
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
medium.feedback: The real interest rate is the price that coordinates saving and investment decisions, and the graph measures it on the vertical axis.

Dashed horizontal and vertical guides connect the labeled intersection points to the axes.

medium.q: What creates demand in the loanable-funds market?
options: Desired investment spending
Current household consumption
The stock of federal debt
Net tax revenue alone
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
medium.feedback: Firms and households demand funds to finance investment projects whose expected returns justify borrowing.

medium.q: What adjustment is expected when the real interest rate is above equilibrium?
options: Excess supply puts downward pressure on the rate
Excess demand puts upward pressure on the rate
Investment demand shifts right automatically
Public saving becomes negative
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
medium.feedback: Above equilibrium, savers offer more funds than investors want, creating downward pressure on the real interest rate.

medium.q: A lower real interest rate by itself causes what change in investment?
options: A rightward shift of investment demand
A movement down along investment demand
A leftward shift of saving supply
A movement up along saving supply
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
medium.feedback: A rate change changes the quantity of investment demanded along the existing curve; it does not shift that curve.

medium.q: New technology raises expected returns on capital at every real interest rate. What changes?
options: There is only movement along investment demand
Saving supply shifts left
The quantity axis shifts
Investment demand shifts right
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
medium.feedback: Higher project profitability is a non-interest determinant of investment demand, so the entire curve shifts right.

medium.q: Businesses become pessimistic about future sales. What is the correct diagrammatic treatment?
options: Investment demand moves downward along itself
Saving supply shifts right
Investment demand shifts left
Saving supply moves upward along itself
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
medium.feedback: Weaker expected sales reduce project profitability at each real rate, shifting investment demand left.

medium.q: The quantity of saving rises after the rate increases, with preferences unchanged. What occurred?
options: A saving-supply shift
An investment-demand shift
Movement along the saving curve
A change in public saving
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
medium.feedback: With no non-interest determinant changing, the rate increase explains a larger quantity supplied along the same curve.

hard.q: Refer to the graph above. At a real interest rate above 8 percent, which comparison does the graph imply?
options: Investment demanded exceeds saving supplied
Saving supplied exceeds investment demanded
Saving and investment remain equal
Both curves shift to the right
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
hard.feedback: Above A, the upward S0 curve lies to the right of D0, so the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded.

The solid blue line labeled D0 (investment) slopes downward through (0, 15) and (140, 8). Point A marks the S0–D0 intersection at (140, 8). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides connect the labeled intersection points to the axes.

hard.q: Refer to the graph above. If the rate moves from 8 percent to 10 percent without any curve shift, what pattern is visible?
options: More saving supplied and less investment demanded
Less saving supplied and more investment demanded
Both saving and investment increase
Both curves shift outward
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
hard.feedback: Moving upward from A travels along both curves: quantity supplied rises while quantity demanded falls.
hard.imageAlt: Loanable-funds graph with S0, D0 and labeled intersection A.

Dashed horizontal and vertical guides connect the labeled intersection points to the axes.

hard.q: A larger budget deficit lowers public saving while private-saving behavior and investment determinants remain unchanged. Which complete loanable-funds sequence follows?
options: National saving falls, investment demand shifts left, and both the rate and quantity fall
National saving rises, supply shifts right, and investment falls along demand
National saving is unchanged because public saving is not part of loanable-funds supply
Supply shifts left, raising the rate and reducing investment
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
hard.feedback: Public saving is part of national saving, which supplies loanable funds. A deficit lowers that supply, raises the equilibrium real interest rate, and crowds out investment along unchanged demand.

hard.q: The real interest rate is above equilibrium with loanable-funds curves unchanged. Which adjustment moves the market back toward equilibrium?
options: Excess investment demand pushes the rate up, increasing the imbalance
Excess saving pushes the rate down toward equilibrium
Saving supply shifts left until all planned investment disappears
Investment demand shifts right because the high rate makes more projects profitable
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
hard.feedback: Above equilibrium, the quantity of funds supplied exceeds the quantity demanded. Downward pressure on the rate causes movements along both curves until planned saving and investment are equal.

hard.q: Households become more willing to save at every real interest rate. The resulting equilibrium rate falls, and firms undertake more projects. Which description separates the initial cause from the response?
options: Investment demand shifts right first; saving rises through movement along unchanged supply
Both saving supply and investment demand shift right merely because their quantities rise
Saving supply shifts right; investment rises through movement down along unchanged demand
The lower rate shifts saving supply left and shifts investment demand right
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
hard.feedback: Greater willingness to save shifts supply right. The lower equilibrium rate then makes more projects profitable, increasing investment as movement along the original investment-demand curve.

hard.q: A retirement incentive increases saving at every real rate, while improved technology raises expected returns on investment. Which conclusion follows without knowing shift sizes?
options: Only saving supply shifts right, so the real rate must fall
Both curves shift right and equilibrium quantity rises; the real-rate direction is ambiguous
Both curves shift right and the real rate must remain unchanged
Saving supply shifts left while investment demand shifts right, so quantity is ambiguous
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
hard.feedback: The saving incentive shifts supply right, while improved technology shifts investment demand right. Both changes raise equilibrium quantity, but their pressures on the real interest rate oppose one another.

elite.q: Refer to the graph above. Treat the displayed curves as straight lines. At a temporary real interest rate of 10 percent, how large is the planned imbalance, and what adjustment returns this market toward A?
options: A 40-unit excess supply; a falling rate shifts both curves toward A
An 80-unit excess supply; a falling rate reduces saving supplied and increases investment demanded
An 80-unit excess demand; a rising rate reduces investment demanded and increases saving supplied
A 40-unit excess demand; a rising rate shifts saving supply right
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
elite.feedback: At 10 percent, S0 supplies 180 units and D0 demands 100, leaving excess supply of 80. A lower rate moves down along S0 and D0 toward their intersection at 140 units and 8 percent; neither curve must shift.
elite.imageAlt: Loanable-funds graph with S0, D0 and labeled intersection A.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is labeled Quantity of loanable funds; the vertical axis is labeled Real interest rate. Coordinates below are (quantity, rate). The quantity axis has no currency scale. All curves are straight. The solid red line labeled S0 (saving) slopes upward through (0, 1) and (140, 8). The solid blue line labeled D0 (investment) slopes downward through (0, 15) and (140, 8). Point A marks the S0–D0 intersection at (140, 8). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides connect the labeled intersection points to the axes.

elite.q: A higher real return encourages households to postpone consumption, while a new retirement incentive increases saving at every real rate. How should these effects be represented?
options: Both changes shift saving supply right because each raises observed saving
Movement along supply, followed by a rightward supply shift
The higher rate shifts supply right, while the incentive causes movement along the curve
Both changes cause movement along the original saving curve because neither affects demand
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
elite.feedback: The current real rate determines a quantity supplied on a given curve. A retirement incentive changes saving behavior at every real rate, so it shifts the whole curve.

elite.q: A saving incentive shifts loanable-funds supply right. The lower equilibrium real rate makes more investment projects profitable, and firms also become more optimistic about future sales. Which description is complete?
options: Both investment increases are movements along demand because firms ultimately borrow more
Both investment increases shift demand because the equilibrium rate changes
The saving incentive shifts investment demand right, while optimism moves firms along that curve
Movement along demand, followed by a separate rightward demand shift
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
elite.feedback: The saving shock lowers the rate and causes movement along the existing investment-demand curve. Optimism changes desired investment at every rate, so it separately shifts demand right.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the graph above. Treat the lines as straight. Starting at A, a technology change shifts D0 horizontally right while S0 stays fixed. The new equilibrium real rate is 10 percent, although the new demand curve is not drawn. What can be inferred about the shift and the quantity response?
options: Demand shifted right by 40 units; equilibrium investment rose by 40 through a rightward shift of S0
Demand shifted right by 80 units; equilibrium investment rose by 80 because saving must match the shift
Demand shifted right by 40 units; equilibrium investment rose by 80 through movement along D0
Demand shifted right by 80 units; equilibrium investment rose by 40 through movement along S0
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
legendaryBoss.feedback: On S0, a 10 percent rate corresponds to 180 units. Old D0 demands 100 units at that rate, so the new demand schedule must be 80 units to the right. Equilibrium investment rises from 140 to 180, or 40 units. The unchanged saving schedule accommodates that quantity through a rate-induced movement; an accounting identity does not force a saving-supply shift.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Loanable-funds graph with S0, D0 and labeled intersection A.

legendaryBoss.q: At a real interest rate below equilibrium, desired investment exceeds desired saving. A student claims this disproves S = I in a closed economy. Which response correctly separates the accounting statement from the market adjustment?
options: Realized saving exceeds realized investment until the rate rises; inventory changes are excluded from investment
Realized investment equals desired investment at every rate; the saving identity applies only after the rate adjusts
Realized saving includes the financing gap as foreign saving; the rate rises until that gap disappears
Realized investment, including unplanned inventories, equals realized saving; excess demand for funds puts upward pressure on the rate
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
legendaryBoss.feedback: S = I is an ex-post closed-economy accounting identity, including inventory investment. Planned quantities can disagree at a posted rate; that behavioral imbalance creates upward pressure on the real rate. Market clearing explains compatible plans, not the validity of the identity.

legendaryBoss.q: Initially, desired investment is I = 300 − 10r, with I in billions of dollars and r measured in percentage points. Technology changes only the intercept. The real rate rises from 4 to 7 percent, and equilibrium investment rises by $20 billion. What happened to investment demand, and what would investment have been at the original rate after the technology change?
options: Demand shifted right by $20 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $280 billion
Demand shifted right by $50 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $310 billion
Demand shifted right by $30 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $290 billion
Demand shifted right by $50 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $280 billion
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Initial investment is 300 − 10(4) = $260 billion, so the new equilibrium quantity is $280 billion. The 3-point rate increase reduces quantity demanded by $30 billion along the new schedule. Technology therefore raises demand by $50 billion at every rate, making investment $310 billion at 4 percent.

repairQuestions.feedback: Borrowers demand funds to finance desired investment, while national saving provides the funds supplied.

repairQuestions.feedback: A change in the market price causes movement along the saving curve, not a shift.

National saving remains unchanged because private saving always offsets a deficit

hard.q: A saving incentive raises planned national saving at every real rate, while weaker expected sales reduce desired investment at every real rate. With upward-sloping saving supply and downward-sloping investment demand, which conclusion and information requirement are correct?

The real rate rises; investment quantity must rise because the saving incentive finances more projects

Saving supply shifts left by $40 billion, but equilibrium investment falls by $20 billion

Saving supply shifts left by $40 billion, and equilibrium investment falls by $40 billion

legendary.q: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion. The straight S0 and S1 curves capture a fiscal change, with the private-saving schedule unchanged and D0 fixed. Starting from B, a second policy raises planned private saving by $15 billion at every real rate. How much must public saving rise from its level at B to restore A?
options: $40 billion; the private-saving incentive cannot change national saving
$5 billion; the required saving shift equals the 20-unit equilibrium-quantity gap
$55 billion; the private-saving increase must be added to the original supply shortfall
$25 billion; together the two changes restore the original saving schedule

Restoring S0 therefore requires $40 billion of additional planned national saving, not merely the 20-unit difference in equilibrium quantity. Private saving supplies $15 billion of that shift, leaving $25 billion of public saving. With D0 fixed, restoring S0 restores A.

A $50 billion increase at every rate; net saving supply and investment demand each move right by $40 billion
A $10 billion increase at every rate; an unchanged interest rate means national saving is unchanged

Since national saving combines private and public saving, the private shift must satisfy private change − 10 = 40, giving +$50 billion. The two shifts leave the depicted equilibrium rate at 6 percent.

easy.q: Trace the loanable-funds mechanism of a larger government deficit, all else equal.
options: Public saving falls, supply shifts left, and the real rate rises
Public saving rises, supply shifts right, and the rate falls
Investment demand shifts right while supply stays fixed
Consumption falls, demand shifts left, and the rate falls

easy.feedback: A deficit lowers public and national saving, reducing loanable-funds supply and raising the equilibrium real interest rate.

easy.q: Why is 'a deficit eliminates all private investment' too strong?
options: Crowding out means investment is lower than otherwise, not necessarily zero
Deficits always reduce the real interest rate
Public saving is unrelated to national saving
Investment demand becomes perfectly vertical
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Government Deficits and Crowding Out.
easy.feedback: The market mechanism reduces equilibrium investment relative to its counterfactual level; the size depends on curves and the saving change.

easy.q: How can more current investment affect future productive capacity?
options: It can enlarge the stock of physical capital
It must reduce every worker's productivity
It converts all capital into consumption
It eliminates depreciation permanently
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment and Capital Formation.
easy.feedback: New structures and equipment add to the capital stock and can raise the economy's future capacity, all else equal.

easy.q: Which statement is appropriately qualified?
options: More investment can raise future capacity, all else equal
More investment always guarantees faster growth
Every investment project succeeds equally
Capital accumulation makes saving unnecessary
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment and Capital Formation.
easy.feedback: Investment contributes to capital formation, but outcomes also depend on project quality, depreciation, technology, and other conditions.

easy.q: If private investment is $30 billion lower because of crowding out, what is the careful growth implication?
options: The existing capital stock immediately falls by $30 billion
Capital formation is lower than it otherwise would be
Long-run output must fall by exactly $30 billion
All future economic growth stops
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment and Capital Formation.
easy.feedback: Crowding out reduces the flow of new capital investment relative to the counterfactual; it does not mechanically erase existing capital.

easy.q: Which statement best describes what the investment-to-capital-formation relationship explains?
options: It explains every determinant of productivity
It derives a complete production function
It isolates one channel from investment to productive capacity
It proves convergence across all economies
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment and Capital Formation.
easy.feedback: The relationship isolates how new investment can add to the capital stock; it does not by itself explain every determinant of productivity or growth.

easy.q: A saving increase lowers the real rate and raises investment. What is the next long-run link?
options: More investment must reduce productive capacity
The real rate becomes a capital good
Saving turns directly into current consumption
More investment can add to the future capital stock
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Investment and Capital Formation.
easy.feedback: The market outcome finances more new capital, which can expand future productive capacity, all else equal.

budget-accounting-and-public-saving.title: Budget Accounting and Public Saving
budget-accounting-and-public-saving.description: Analyze budget balances, revenues, outlays, public saving, and fiscal accounting identities.

easy.q: When federal outlays exceed federal revenues during a fiscal year, what is the result?
options: A budget deficit
A budget surplus
A balanced budget
A reduction in gross debt
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
easy.feedback: A deficit occurs because annual outlays are greater than annual revenues.

easy.q: Which fiscal position exists when annual federal revenues exceed annual outlays?
options: A budget deficit
A budget surplus
A balanced budget
A debt rollover
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
easy.feedback: Revenues greater than outlays produce a positive budget balance, called a surplus.

easy.q: Why is federal borrowing not classified as federal revenue in budget accounting?
options: It counts as revenue when interest rates fall
It becomes a transfer payment received by households
It finances a shortfall rather than counting as revenue
It is included in government purchases when debt is issued
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
easy.feedback: Debt issuance supplies financing, but it does not turn the borrowed funds into budget revenue.

easy.q: In the identity public saving = T − G, what must T represent in this accounting framework?
options: Net tax revenue after relevant transfers
Total federal outlays including transfers and net interest
Gross tax collections before subtracting any transfer payments
The accumulated federal debt stock at a specific date
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
easy.feedback: The shorthand is valid here only when T is defined net of transfers and G is government purchases.

easy.q: Under public saving = T − G, with T defined as net tax revenue and G as government purchases, what does negative public saving mean?
options: Private saving must also be below zero
T is less than G
Nominal GDP must be declining during the year
The government can have no outstanding federal debt
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
easy.feedback: Public saving is negative when net tax revenue T is below government purchases G.

easy.q: A Social Security benefit payment is best classified as what from the federal budget perspective?
options: Federal revenue from payroll taxes
Government purchases included in GDP when paid
Intragovernmental holdings of federal debt
A transfer payment within federal outlays
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
easy.feedback: The payment is an outlay that transfers income; it is not a purchase of current output when issued.

easy.q: The federal government buys newly produced rescue equipment. How is the transaction classified?
options: An outlay and a government purchase
A transfer payment without a current purchase
Federal revenue
Debt held by the public
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
easy.feedback: Paying for newly produced equipment is both an outlay and government purchases in GDP.

medium.q: Federal revenues are $4.8 trillion and outlays are $6.2 trillion. Using revenues minus outlays, what is the budget balance?
options: +$1.4 trillion
−$11.0 trillion
+$11.0 trillion
−$1.4 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
medium.feedback: Revenues minus outlays equals $4.8 trillion minus $6.2 trillion, or −$1.4 trillion, a deficit.

medium.q: A federal budget balance is reported as +$120 billion. What does the positive sign mean?
options: Revenues exceed outlays by $120 billion
Outlays exceed revenues by $120 billion
Federal debt equals $120 billion
Borrowing increased by exactly $120 billion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
medium.feedback: Under the stated revenues-minus-outlays convention, a positive balance is a surplus.

medium.q: Federal revenues total $5.1 trillion and outlays total $5.9 trillion. What is the deficit expressed as a positive magnitude?
options: −$0.8 trillion
$0.8 trillion
$5.1 trillion
$11.0 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
medium.feedback: Outlays exceed revenues by $0.8 trillion, so the deficit magnitude is reported as positive $0.8 trillion.

medium.q: Net tax revenue T is $3.2 trillion and government purchases G are $3.8 trillion. What is public saving?
options: +$0.6 trillion
$3.2 trillion
−$0.6 trillion
$7.0 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
medium.feedback: Using the stated identity, public saving is T minus G, or $3.2 trillion minus $3.8 trillion.

medium.q: Suppose T is explicitly defined as net tax revenue and equals $2.9 trillion, while government purchases G equal $2.5 trillion. What is public saving?
options: −$0.4 trillion
$2.5 trillion
$5.4 trillion
+$0.4 trillion
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
medium.feedback: With the variables defined, T − G equals +$0.4 trillion, indicating positive public saving.

medium.q: Which statement accurately distinguishes mandatory and discretionary spending?
options: Mandatory spending cannot change
Mandatory follows standing law; discretionary depends on appropriations
Discretionary spending has no economically important uses
Every federal transfer payment belongs to discretionary spending
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
medium.feedback: The labels describe budget processes, not whether spending matters or can ever be changed by law.

medium.q: Interest paid on outstanding federal debt belongs in which budget category?
options: Federal revenue from outstanding Treasury securities
A transfer payment counted as government purchases in GDP
Net interest outlays, not government purchases
Intragovernmental holdings in federal trust-fund accounts
medium.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
medium.feedback: Interest outlays service prior borrowing; they are not purchases of newly produced goods and services.

hard.q: One table reports a budget balance of −$900 billion; another describes a deficit of $900 billion. Are the reports consistent?
options: No; both reports must show the shortfall with a negative sign
No; balance and deficit figures cannot have the same magnitude
Yes; one is signed and the other gives the deficit magnitude
Yes; both figures describe a $900 billion budget surplus
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
hard.feedback: A negative revenues-minus-outlays balance and a positive deficit magnitude can describe the same shortfall.

hard.q: Revenues rise from $4.9 trillion to $5.2 trillion while outlays rise from $6.0 trillion to $6.1 trillion. How does the budget balance change?
options: It worsens by $0.2 trillion
It improves by $0.3 trillion and becomes a budget surplus
It remains unchanged as both rise
It improves by $0.2 trillion but remains negative
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
hard.feedback: The balance moves from −$1.1 trillion to −$0.9 trillion, an improvement of $0.2 trillion.

hard.q: A table gives total federal revenues of $5 trillion and total outlays, including transfers and interest, of $6 trillion. What should revenues minus outlays be called?
options: A $1 trillion federal budget deficit
Public saving of −$1 trillion under T − G
Private saving of $1 trillion
Government purchases of $6 trillion
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
hard.feedback: Total revenues minus total outlays is the budget balance. In the T − G public-saving shorthand, T must be net tax revenue and G must be government purchases.

hard.q: Holding the relevant definitions and other items fixed, what is the basic public-saving implication of a larger budget deficit?
options: Public saving is necessarily higher
Public saving is lower
Private saving becomes zero by identity
Government purchases are no longer part of GDP
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
hard.feedback: A wider fiscal shortfall reduces the government's contribution to national saving under the introductory accounting link.

hard.q: A benefit payment and a purchase of new federal vehicles are both outlays. What distinguishes their GDP treatment?
options: Both enter G
Neither enters GDP
Only the benefit payment enters G directly when Treasury pays it
Only the vehicle purchase enters G when paid
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
hard.feedback: A transfer redistributes income, whereas the vehicle purchase pays for current production.

hard.q: Taxes raise $4.7 trillion and borrowing supplies $1.1 trillion. Which amount is federal revenue?
options: $4.7 trillion
$1.1 trillion
$5.8 trillion
Neither amount
hard.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
hard.feedback: Taxes are receipts; borrowing finances the gap and is not recorded as revenue.

elite.q: A published table rounds revenues to $5.6 trillion, outlays to $7.4 trillion, and the deficit to $1.9 trillion. Why need the rounded entries not subtract exactly?
options: The displayed figures were rounded independently
The deficit excludes displayed revenues
Borrowing is added to both displayed revenues and displayed outlays
The deficit uses calendar-year data
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
elite.feedback: Independent rounding can make displayed components differ slightly from an identity calculated with unrounded values.

elite.q: A budget worksheet reports $920 billion of cash inflows, including $180 billion from issuing new debt, and $870 billion of total outlays. All remaining inflows are revenues; there are no other financing adjustments. What are the budget balance and the amount of new borrowing left to increase cash balances?
options: A $50 billion surplus and no borrowing needed for the outlays
A $130 billion deficit and a $50 billion cash increase
A $130 billion deficit and a $180 billion cash increase
A $310 billion deficit and a $130 billion cash decrease
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
elite.feedback: Revenues exclude borrowing: 920 − 180 = $740 billion. Revenues minus outlays equal 740 − 870 = −$130 billion. Of the $180 billion borrowed, $130 billion finances the deficit and $50 billion increases cash balances.

elite.q: A simplified fiscal account reports gross tax receipts of $900 billion, transfers of $180 billion, government purchases of $660 billion and interest payments of $70 billion. These are all revenues and outlays. For this exercise define T as gross taxes minus transfers, excluding interest. Which pair gives textbook public saving T − G and the full budget balance?
options: Public saving is $240 billion; the full budget has a $60 billion surplus
Public saving is −$10 billion; the full budget also has a $10 billion deficit
Public saving is $60 billion; the full budget has a $10 billion deficit
Public saving is $60 billion; the full budget has a $60 billion surplus
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
elite.feedback: Under the stated convention, T = 900 − 180 = $720 billion and T − G = $60 billion. Total outlays are 180 + 660 + 70 = $910 billion, giving a $10 billion deficit. The $70 billion difference is interest, which this exercise excludes from net taxes. Transfers are already deducted in T and must not be deducted a second time.

elite.q: A speaker calls all discretionary outlays “optional” and all mandatory outlays “uncontrollable.” What is wrong with the claim?
options: Discretionary outlays are made without any congressional appropriations
The labels describe funding rules, not permanence or importance
Mandatory programs never transfer
Net interest outlays are classified as federal budget revenues
elite.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
elite.feedback: Process labels do not settle importance, desirability, or whether future law can alter spending.

legendary.q: A government starts the year with $3,600 billion of debt. Revenues are $760 billion and outlays are $940 billion. It issues $500 billion of debt, including debt used to repay $270 billion of maturing principal; remaining financing may change cash balances. With no other debt or financing adjustments, which reconciliation is correct?
options: A $180 billion deficit, ending debt of $4,100 billion, and a $320 billion increase in cash
A $320 billion surplus, ending debt of $3,830 billion, and a $50 billion increase in cash
A $180 billion deficit, ending debt of $3,830 billion, and a $50 billion increase in cash
A $450 billion deficit, ending debt of $3,780 billion, and unchanged cash
legendary.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
legendary.feedback: The deficit is 940 − 760 = $180 billion; debt issuance is financing, not revenue. Net issuance is 500 − 270 = $230 billion, so ending debt is $3,830 billion. Net financing exceeds the deficit by $50 billion, increasing cash. Principal repayment is not counted again as a budget outlay.

boss.q: Annual federal revenues equal $5.0 trillion and outlays equal $5.3 trillion. Which fiscal position is shown?
options: A $0.3 trillion surplus
A balanced budget
A $5.3 trillion debt stock
A $0.3 trillion deficit
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
boss.feedback: Outlays exceed revenues by $0.3 trillion, so the annual budget is in deficit.

boss.q: According to CBO's February 2026 baseline, FY2026 revenues are projected at about $5.6 trillion and outlays at about $7.4 trillion. What fiscal position is projected?
options: A deficit because projected outlays exceed projected revenues
A surplus because projected revenues are positive
A balanced budget because both values are projections
A debt stock of $1.8 trillion
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
boss.feedback: CBO projects outlays above revenues, which is a deficit; the published rounded deficit is about $1.9 trillion.

boss.q: With T defined as net tax revenue and G as government purchases, T equals $800 billion and G equals $900 billion. What is public saving?
options: +$100 billion
$800 billion
$1.7 trillion
−$100 billion
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
boss.feedback: T − G equals −$100 billion, so public saving is negative.

boss.q: Which statement uses the public-saving convention correctly?
options: T − G, with T net of transfers and G purchases
Total revenues minus all federal outlays is always T − G public saving
T means gross collections and G includes transfers
Public saving is the federal debt stock
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
boss.feedback: The notation is valid only when T is net tax revenue, net of transfers, and G is government purchases.

boss.q: The government collects payroll taxes, sends pension benefits, and buys medical equipment. Which classification is correct?
options: Taxes, benefits, and equipment purchases are all federal revenue
Benefits and equipment both enter government purchases in GDP when paid
Taxes are revenue; both payments are outlays; only equipment is G
Payroll taxes are borrowing
boss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
boss.feedback: Budget and GDP classifications overlap but are not identical: transfers are outlays without entering G when paid.

legendaryBoss.q: A simplified government has only three outlay categories: purchases of current domestic goods and services, transfers, and interest. Purchases rise from $400 billion to $430 billion, transfers from $300 billion to $350 billion, and interest from $50 billion to $70 billion. Revenues rise by $60 billion. Which comparison is correct?
options: The deficit widens by $40 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $100 billion
The deficit narrows by $30 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $40 billion
The deficit widens by $100 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $30 billion
The deficit widens by $40 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $30 billion
legendaryBoss.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Outlays rise by 30 + 50 + 20 = $100 billion. With revenues up $60 billion, the deficit widens $40 billion. Only the $30 billion increase in current purchases directly increases G; transfers and interest are budget outlays without being current government purchases. No induced output response is being calculated.

repairQuestions.q: Federal revenues are $5 trillion and outlays are $6 trillion. Is the budget in surplus or deficit?
options: Surplus
Deficit
Balanced
Debt-free
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
repairQuestions.feedback: Outlays exceed revenues by $1 trillion, so the federal budget is in deficit.

repairQuestions.q: T is net tax revenue of $700 billion and G is purchases of $600 billion. What is public saving?
options: −$100 billion
+$100 billion
$600 billion
$1.3 trillion
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
repairQuestions.feedback: Subtract government purchases from net tax revenue: $700 billion minus $600 billion equals +$100 billion.

repairQuestions.q: Which transaction is a government purchase rather than a transfer?
options: The federal purchase of new computers
A pension benefit payment
An unemployment benefit payment
An interest payment on debt
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
repairQuestions.feedback: Buying current goods is a government purchase; benefits and interest are outlays but not G purchases.

bridgeQuestions.q: A federal budget records revenues below outlays. What financing issue follows from that accounting result?
options: The shortfall becomes additional tax revenue in the same year
Government purchases become zero
The shortfall must be financed, commonly through borrowing
Existing federal debt disappears
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A deficit is an annual financing gap; borrowing is a common way to cover it.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does negative public saving matter beyond the federal budget?
options: It directly fixes the economy's nominal exchange rate
It makes positive private saving impossible by definition
It reduces one component of national saving
It determines the national money supply without monetary policy
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Negative public saving lowers national saving, all else equal, and therefore reduces the funds available to finance investment in the loanable-funds model.

bridgeQuestions.q: A federal benefit payment is an outlay but not government purchases in GDP when paid. When can it affect measured GDP?
options: When Treasury classifies the benefit as mandatory spending
When recipients buy newly produced goods or services
Immediately, because every federal outlay enters G in GDP
Only after the outstanding federal debt stock begins to fall
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The transfer itself is not production; later consumption of current final output can enter GDP.

deficits-debt-and-government-borrowing.title: Deficits, Debt, and Government Borrowing
deficits-debt-and-government-borrowing.description: Distinguish deficits from debt and analyze persistent deficits and government borrowing.

easy.q: Which statement correctly classifies the federal deficit and federal debt?
options: Deficit and debt: both annual fiscal flows
Deficit and debt: both accumulated fiscal stocks
Deficit: accumulated stock; debt: annual flow
Deficit: annual flow; debt: accumulated stock
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
easy.feedback: A deficit is measured over a period, while debt is measured at a point in time.

easy.q: The federal deficit falls from $1.8 trillion to $1.2 trillion. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Borrowing needs are smaller, but debt can still rise
Federal debt falls by the $0.6 trillion reduction in the deficit
The budget moves into surplus
Existing federal debt is eliminated
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
easy.feedback: A smaller positive deficit adds less to debt than before, but it still represents a shortfall.

easy.q: What does a balanced annual federal budget imply about existing federal debt?
options: It immediately reduces the accumulated debt stock to zero
It prevents a new deficit but does not erase existing debt
It proves the preceding fiscal year ended with a surplus
It reclassifies all existing federal debt as current revenue
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Deficit Versus Debt.
easy.feedback: Balancing annual revenues and outlays addresses the current flow, not the accumulated stock.

easy.q: What generally happens when the federal government runs persistent deficits?
options: They automatically erase existing debt
Every annual deficit becomes an equal surplus in a later year
They generally add to accumulated debt
Government purchases are removed from measured GDP during deficit years
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
easy.feedback: Deficits are recurring gaps that generally require financing and add to the debt stock.

easy.q: Which sequence is correct at an introductory level?
options: Surplus, lower revenue, larger deficit by definition
Debt, automatic revenue, no outlays
Borrowing, smaller debt, larger surplus by identity
Deficit, financing through borrowing, larger accumulated debt
easy.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing.
easy.feedback: Borrowing commonly finances a deficit, and repeated borrowing adds to outstanding debt.
